questions: Nicknamed "The Flying Finn," this ski jumper won four Olympic golds — three of them at a single 1988 Games — making him one of the sport's greatest ever. Who was he?

In early 1258, after provocations from caliph al-Musta'sim, a Mongol army under Hulegu took and sacked the Abbasid capital — an event long seen as the end of the Islamic Golden Age. What is this event called?
Siege of Baghdad: Mongol conquest of the Abbasid Caliphate (1258)
Its Syriac name means simply 'sword' — the mass murder and deportation of Assyrian and Syriac Christians by Ottoman forces during World War I. What is this genocide called?

Sparked by a 1962 coup that toppled a newly crowned king and proclaimed a republic — and even abolished slavery — this conflict pitted royalists backed near the Saudi border against the new government. Which war was it?
He was slated to be the sixth person to walk on the Moon, but his lunar landing was aborted en route — making him today the last surviving crew member of Apollo 13. Who is this astronaut?

A leader of the 1897 Cretan Revolt who helped win Crete's autonomy and then its union with Greece, this statesman served as Greek prime minister across eight terms over more than twelve years. Who was he?
Ruled from the ancient city of Zafar near modern Sanaa, this kingdom of Yemen's southern highlands eventually swallowed up its neighbors Saba', Qataban, and Hadramaut — which polity?
Himyar: Former kingdom in ancient Yemen
This historical region of northeastern Greater Iran became the political and cultural base of the Parni people and the Arsacid dynasty — lending its name to a famous empire. Which region?
Parthia: Historical region located in northeastern Iran
A Founding Father who signed the Treaty of Paris and directed U.S. foreign policy through much of the 1780s, he became the very first chief justice of the United States in 1789 — who was he?

This Sanskrit term translating as 'emptiness' or 'voidness' anchors a key Mahāyāna Buddhist tenet, and in Theravāda often points to the non-self nature of the five aggregates of experience — what is it?
Śūnyatā: Philosophical concept of emptiness found in Asian religions

A vaudeville-trained humorist born a citizen of the Cherokee Nation and known as 'Oklahoma's Favorite Son,' he made 71 films and wrote over 4,000 newspaper columns before dying in a 1935 plane crash — who was he?
Will Rogers: American humorist and entertainer (1879–1935)

Caused by the spiral bacterium Treponema pallidum, this infection famously announces itself with a single painless ulcer called a chancre, then a rash that loves the palms and soles — which sexually transmitted disease is it?
Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum subspecies pallidum.

The brightest star in the constellation Aquila and a vertex of the Summer Triangle, this nearby A-type star spins so fast — about 286 km/s at its equator — that it bulges noticeably. Which star is it?
Altair: Brightest star in the constellation Aquila

Sometimes called "radiology done inside out," this medical specialty records radiation emitted from within the body and emphasizes function over anatomy — using scans like SPECT and PET. What's the field?
Often silent at first, this disease arises from an ovary or nearby structures and announces itself only later with bloating, pelvic pain, and abdominal swelling — what is it?
Ovarian cancer is a cancerous tumor of an ovary.
This sugar alcohol pulls double duty as a low-calorie sweetener and a drug given by injection to lower pressure in the eyes or inside the skull — an osmotic diuretic. What is it?
Also called oxolane, this colorless, water-miscible cyclic ether is a versatile solvent and polymer precursor — and an isomer of butanone. Abbreviated with three letters, what is it?
Also called androgenetic alopecia, this condition driven by male sex hormones and genetics shows up as a receding hairline or a thinning crown in men — what's the common name for it?
Fill in the blank: “____ is an inorganic, monatomic anion of fluorine, with the chemical formula F (also written), whose salts are typically white or colorless.”
Fluoride is an inorganic, monatomic anion of fluorine, with the chemical formula F (also written), whose salts are typically white or colorless.
This biological process unfolds in predictable phases — hemostasis, inflammation, cell proliferation, and tissue remodeling — to replace damaged skin after the barrier is broken. What is it?
Wound healing refers to a living organism's replacement of destroyed or damaged tissue by newly produced tissue.
One of America's top rocketry and high-speed-flight experts, this engineer helped found engineering cybernetics before being deported to China in 1955. Who was he?

Qian Xuesen (December 11, 1911 - October 31, 2009; also spelled as Tsien Hsue-shen) was a Chinese aerospace engineer and cyberneticist who made significant contributions to the field of aerodynamics and established engineering cybernetics.
This medium-sized antelope of India and Nepal sports corkscrew horns up to 30 inches long and a striking two-tone coat, with white around the eyes set against black face stripes — which animal?
Blackbuck: Antelope native to India and Nepal
In young children it can mean ear-pulling, extra crying, and poor sleep; it's a group of inflammatory diseases of the middle ear, from acute infections to lingering fluid. What's the medical name?
Otitis media: Inflammation of the middle ear
Struck off the medical register for 'serious professional misconduct,' this former surgeon authored the fraudulent 1998 Lancet paper falsely tying the MMR vaccine to autism — who is he?
This South Korean actor-turned-businessman starred in the 2002 drama Winter Sonata — a cornerstone of the Korean Wave — before retiring from acting and chairing a talent agency. Who is he?

Written by Jimmy Perry and David Croft and pulling in 18 million viewers, this BBC sitcom followed the Home Guard volunteers too old, unwell, or exempt to fight in WWII — hence its title. What was the show?
She captained both the 'Fierce Five' and the 'Final Five' U.S. women's Olympic gymnastics teams to gold, and at London 2012 became the most decorated American gymnast of those Games. Who is she?
Aly Raisman (born May 25, 1994) is an American retired artistic gymnast and two-time Olympian.

With 147 professional wins and ten Grand Tour victories — including five Tours de France — this Breton cyclist sits just one Grand Tour behind Merckx, and no rider since has won more than seven. Who is he?

At just 14 he became the youngest male ever to swim for Australia, and went on to win five Olympic golds — three of them as the standout star of the 2000 Sydney Games in his hometown. Who is this freestyle great?
Fill in the blank: “____ is an American multinational corporation headquartered in Midland, Michigan, United States.”
Dow Chemical Company is an American multinational corporation headquartered in Midland, Michigan, United States.

John Cage's 1952 composition for any instrument has a score that simply instructs the performers not to play — leaving the audience to hear only ambient sound across three movements. What's this famously silent piece?

Central to Indian classical music, this melodic framework — its name literally means "colouring" or "dyeing" — gives a musician structure to improvise within while aiming to "colour the mind." What is it?
Raga: Melodic mode of improvisation in Indian music

Built around McCartney's vocal, acoustic guitar, and a string quartet — essentially the Beatles' first solo performance — this 1965 track has been recorded some 2,200 times, among the most-covered in history. Which song is it?
Born Giovanni Battista Lulli, this Italian-born master of the French Baroque spent his life at Louis XIV's court and collaborated with Molière on works like 'Le Bourgeois gentilhomme.' Who was he?
Jean-Baptiste Lully (born Giovanni Battista Lulli; 28 or 29 November [O.S.
This Texas-born journalist became a national name in 1961 when his Hurricane Carla reporting saved thousands, then was reporting from Dallas the day JFK was assassinated — who is he?

Charlotte Perkins Gilman's 1892 short story — told through the journal of a woman confined to an upstairs room by her physician husband — is praised both as early feminist literature and as superb horror. What's its title?
The Yellow Wallpaper: 1892 short story by Charlotte Perkins Gilman
His motto was "Learning by head, hand and heart," and this Swiss educational reformer is credited with all but wiping out illiteracy in Switzerland by 1830 — who was he?
Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi: Swiss pedagogue and educational reformer (1746–1827)
Nicknamed "The Bean," this seamless, mirror-polished sculpture of 168 welded stainless-steel plates by Anish Kapoor is the centerpiece of Chicago's Millennium Park — what is it?
Cloud Gate: Sculpture by Anish Kapoor in Chicago

Executed in 1536, this English scholar produced the first English scriptures drawn straight from Hebrew and Greek, the first to use the printing press, and the first to render God's name as "Jehovah" — who was he?
William Tyndale: English biblical scholar, translator, and reformer (1494–1536)
First printed in the Atlantic Monthly in August 1915, this Robert Frost poem about diverging paths — literal and figurative — is famously open to wildly different interpretations. What's its title?
The Road Not Taken: 1915 poem by Robert Frost
A self-described feminist who's nonetheless a fierce critic of contemporary American feminism and post-structuralism, she wrote the sweeping 1990 study Sexual Personae — who is she?
Camille Paglia: American feminist academic and critic (born 1947)
This Russian writer is best remembered for the novels 'The Duel' and 'Yama: The Pit,' along with the story 'The Garnet Bracelet,' later made into a 1965 film. Who was he?
A staple from the Caribbean to Oceania to East Asia, this Araceae-family plant is prized for the starchy underground corm it grows much like a yam — what is it?
Holding the title of smallest great ape, this creature has pinker lips and a darker face than its close cousin, and was once dismissed as merely a 'pygmy' subspecies of it — what is it?
Born in 1900 in the Saratov Governorate, this beloved Soviet contralto built her fame on performing Russian folk songs — who was she?
A close ally of Robespierre, this French revolutionary chose suicide over arrest when authorities stormed the Hôtel de Ville during the coup of 9–10 Thermidor — who was he?
Once crowned the 'Hop King of the World' and the first mayor of Puyallup, this pioneer kept retracing the Oregon Trail by ox-wagon to preserve its memory — who was he?
Between 1968 and 1976 this Japanese gymnast collected twelve Olympic medals — eight of them gold — making him his country's most decorated Olympian by golds. Who is he?
Sawao Katō is a Japanese former gymnast and one of the most successful Olympic athletes of all time.

Sent to Lakehurst in 1937 with unusual new recording gear to cover an airship's landing, this American radio reporter delivered a charged on-air account of the Hindenburg disaster that became a broadcasting landmark. Who is he?
Herbert Morrison was an American journalist whose charged radio report on the Hindenburg disaster is recognized as a landmark in broadcasting.
Written on clay tablets as early as 2600 BCE, this Sumerian liturgy to the goddess Nintud ranks among the oldest surviving literature in the world. What is it?
Liturgy to Nintud on the creation of man and woman
Kesh temple hymn: Oldest surviving literary text in the world
Born in 1559, this classical scholar and philologist worked first in France and then in England, and fathered a fellow classical scholar, Méric. Who is he?
Isaac Casaubon (18 February 1559 - 1 July 1614) was a classical scholar and philologist, first in France and then later in England.

Dukkha, samudaya, nirodha — this Buddhist quartet lays out 'how things really are when seen correctly,' beginning with the claim that all transient existence is suffering — what is this set of teachings called?
In Buddhism, the Four Noble Truths are "the truths of the noble one (the Buddha)," a statement of how things really are when they are seen correctly.
Spelling out as Na-Ma-Shi-Va-Ya, this five-syllable Hindu mantra is the most important in Shaivism and offers salutations to 'the auspicious one' — what is it?
Carved out of the Carolingian Empire at the Treaty of Verdun in 843 and lasting until the Capetians took over in 987, which kingdom was the very first stage of what we now call France?
West Francia: Predecessor of France from 843 to 987
Founded in 698 by Tae Choyŏng and originally called the Kingdom of Jin, which multiethnic realm once spanned Northeast China, the northern Korean Peninsula, and the Russian Far East?
Parhae: 7th-10th century kingdom in East Asia
The daughter of an Imperial Russian general, she served as People's Commissar for Welfare and became the first woman in history to sit in a national cabinet — who was this Bolshevik?
Known to the CIA and Hmong veterans as the 'Secret War,' this Cold War proxy conflict pitted the Communist Pathet Lao against the Royal Lao Government from 1959 to 1975 — what was it?
Laotian Civil War: 1959–1975 conflict in Laos
Pulled from the Apollo 13 crew three days before launch, this astronaut then helped guide the crippled ship home before flying to the Moon himself on Apollo 16 — who is it?
House speaker, secretary of state, and a three-time loser of the presidency, this Kentuckian earned the nickname 'the Great Compromiser' for defusing sectional crises — who was he?
Henry Clay (April 12, 1777 - June 29, 1852) was an American lawyer, statesman, and diplomat who represented Kentucky in both the United States House of Representatives and the United States Senate.
Beginning in October 1990, this conflict pitted the government's army against the Patriotic Front, a refugee-founded rebel force led in part by Paul Kagame, and ran until July 1994 — what was it?
Rwandan Civil War: 1990–1994 armed struggle in Rwanda
It erupted in December 2013 when President Kiir accused his former deputy Riek Machar of plotting a coup, sparking five years of ethnic massacres and mass displacement — which war was this?
The South Sudanese Civil War was a multi-sided civil war in South Sudan fought from 2013 to 2018 between government and opposition forces.
Founded around 1399 and ruled mostly by the Wadiyars, this southern Indian realm began as a vassal of the Vijayanagara Empire and endured all the way until 1950 — what was it?
Kingdom of Mysore: Monarchy in India (1399–1947)
A broad-spectrum benzimidazole drug, it clears out an alarming roll call of intestinal parasites — pinworm, hookworm, ascariasis, giardiasis and more. Which medication is it?
Rooted in Minangkabau cooking at the crossroads of the Malacca Strait, this dish slow-cooks meat in spiced coconut milk until the oil separates and it fries in its own glaze — what is it?
The famous AL 288-1 skeleton nicknamed 'Lucy,' unearthed in Ethiopia's Afar region, belongs to which extinct East African hominin species that lived roughly 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago?
Australopithecus afarensis: Extinct hominid from the Pliocene of East Africa
Its name comes from the Greek for 'thin,' and this hormone made mainly by fat cells tells the brain how full your energy reserves are, shaping appetite and satiety — what is it?

Spanning everything from sacred religious writings to the exuberantly profane, and often grouped by place, language, and genre, what broad body of European writing falls between late antiquity and the Renaissance?
Medieval literature: Literary works of the Middle Ages
The sole living member of its genus, this slender, long-legged antelope of southwest Africa sports a white face, a dark eye-to-mouth stripe, and backward-curving horns on both sexes — what is it?
Springbok: Antelope of southwest and south Africa

This colourless, water-mixable lab solvent is technically odorless — but degraded samples reek of fish thanks to a dimethylamine impurity. It's better known by a three-letter abbreviation; what's the compound?
A self-taught rocketeer and practicing occultist, this co-founder of both JPL and Aerojet invented the first castable composite rocket propellant before dying young in 1952. Who was he?
One of the largest parasitoid wasps, this creature paralyzes its eight-legged prey with a sting, drags it into a nest, and lays a single egg so the larva can devour the still-living host. What is it?
Tarantula hawk: Common name for two genera of wasps
Catalyzed in nature by iron-bearing nitrogenase enzymes and famously partnered with legumes, this process turns molecular N2 into ammonia — what's it called?
Nitrogen fixation is a chemical process by which molecular dinitrogen (N2) is converted into ammonia (NH3).
Set in Yorkshire and running on the BBC from 1973 all the way to 2010, this Roy Clarke sitcom racked up 295 episodes across 31 series — making it a record-setting comedy. What's it called?
Last of the Summer Wine: British TV sitcom (1973–2010)
"Live Free or Die" is the motto of this seventh-smallest state, the "Granite State" of New England with Concord as its capital — which one?
Since 1782 this riotously gilded complex at the heart of Bangkok has been the official residence of the Kings of Siam, and it still hosts state ceremonies today — which landmark is it?
Grand Palace: Royal residence in Bangkok, Thailand
Played since at least 1650 BCE and likely resembling racquetball, this ritual-laced ancient sport survives today as a game called ulama in parts of Mexico — what is it?

The Mesoamerican ballgame was a sport with ritual associations played since at least 1650 BCE (the middle Mesoamerican Preclassic period of the pre-Columbian era) by the people of Ancient Mesoamerica.

A speedy, creative forward for CSKA Moscow named the Soviet league's MVP in 1972 and 1973, this Russian is rated among the greatest hockey players ever — though his career ended at his death in 1981; who was he?
Valeri Kharlamov (14 January 1948 - 27 August 1981) was a Russian ice hockey forward who played for CSKA Moscow in the Soviet League from 1967 until his death in 1981.
An aggressive batsman and swing bowler, this English all-rounder played twice in losing World Cup finals, later chaired Durham, and now sits in the House of Lords — who is it?
This middle-Baroque German organist advanced the chorale prelude and fugue and trained many pupils, yet today he's remembered chiefly for a single Canon in D — who was he?

Born in South London in the early 2000s as a UK garage offshoot, this dark, bass-heavy genre got its name and early airplay at Plastic People's "Forward" night and on pirate station Rinse FM — what is it?
Dubstep: Genre of electronic dance music that originated in South London

In the Bronx in 1973, this Jamaican-American DJ used two copies of the same record to stretch out the drum "break" — a trick that birthed hip-hop and earned him the title Father of the genre. Who is he?
Known at the time as the 'New Negro Movement,' this 1920s–30s flowering of African-American music, art, and literature centered on one Manhattan neighborhood — what's it called?
First published in 1892, this collection gathered the earliest short stories of a consulting detective, all narrated by Dr. Watson after running monthly in The Strand Magazine — what's its title?
The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes: Collection of short stories by Arthur Conan Doyle
Set in 1906 Indian Territory and based on the play 'Green Grow the Lilacs,' this first-ever Rodgers and Hammerstein musical ran an unprecedented 2,212 Broadway performances — what's it called?
Oklahoma!: Musical by Rodgers and Hammerstein
This American investigative journalist is best known for his 1996 'Dark Alliance' series linking Nicaraguan Contra rebels to the rise of the L.A. crack cocaine trade — who is it?
Crowned the 2010 Olympic figure skating champion and dubbed 'Queen' by her fans, this two-time World champion is regarded as one of the greatest skaters in South Korean history — who is it?
Yuna Kim: South Korean figure skater (born 1990)

Born Ali-Muhammad in Shiraz in 1819, this Iranian religious leader founded Babism and claimed to be a Manifestation of God on par with Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad — his chosen title meant "the gate." Who was he?
The sole species in its genus and a fixture of Mediterranean gardens, this drought-and-flood-tolerant shrub of the dogbane family is also called rose laurel or rosebay — what is it?

Growing in the brutal heat of the Namib desert, this Angolan and Namibian oddity sprouts just two leaves from a single woody stem for its entire life — and is the lone living genus of its whole family. What plant is it?
Welwitschia is a monotypic genus of gnetophytes containing only the species welwitschia mirabilis.
First unearthed in 1994 in Spain's Gran Dolina cave, this Early Pleistocene human was named 'pioneer man' because it was among the first to settle Western Europe. Which species is it?

Homo antecessor (Latin for 'pioneer man') is an extinct species of archaic human recorded in the Spanish Sierra de Atapuerca, a productive archaeological site, from 1.2 to 0.8 million years ago during the Early Pleistocene.
Fill in the blank: “____ was one of the Thirteen Colonies that first formed the United States.”
History of South Carolina was one of the Thirteen Colonies that first formed the United States.
An English dyer and astronomer, this man's 1729 experiments were the first to systematically show that electricity could travel through metals and appear on the surface of insulators — who was he?
Stephen Gray was an English dyer and astronomer who was the first to systematically experiment with electrical conduction.

Because this element has a full electron shell, the highest first ionization energy of any element, and almost no electron affinity, chemists long assumed it simply couldn't bond — what kind of substances were thought impossible?

Helium is the smallest and the lightest noble gas and one of the most unreactive elements, so it was commonly assumed that helium compounds could not exist at all, or at least not under normal conditions.

Fox-sized and found on every continent but Australia and Antarctica, these primitive ornithischian dinosaurs are known for odd teeth — canine-like tusks plus cheek teeth built for chewing. What's this family?
Heterodontosauridae is a family of ornithischian dinosaurs that were likely among the most basal (primitive) members of the group.
In 1990 this British sports journalist became the first woman to present the BBC's 'Grandstand,' having earlier helped bring American football to British television — who is she?

Helen Rollason (ne Grindley; 11 March 1956 - 9 August 1999) was a British sports journalist and television presenter, who in 1990 became the first female presenter of the BBC's sports programme Grandstand.
Spread across five floors and 472,900 square feet with simulated dinosaur habitats, a carousel, and a steam locomotive, this Indiana institution is the largest of its kind in the world — what is it?
The Children's Museum of Indianapolis is the world's largest children's museum.
Australia's first cricketer of real significance, this man also helped found Australian rules football, having learned rugby and cricket as captain at England's Rugby School — who is he?
Tom Wills (19 August 1835 - 2 May 1880) was an Australian sportsman who is credited with being Australia's first cricketer of significance and a founder of Australian rules football.
Despite serious visual impairment and a famed photographic memory, this 19th-century scholar of Renaissance Spain is recognized as the first American scientific historian — who is he?
William H. Prescott (May 4, 1796 - January 28, 1859) was an American historian and Hispanist, who is widely recognized by historiographers to have been the first American scientific historian.

Charles I of Spain awarded this navigator a coat of arms reading "Primus circumdedisti me" — "You were the first to circumnavigate me" — after he completed the first voyage around the Earth aboard the Victoria. Who was he?
Juan Sebastián Elcano: Spanish seafarer and circumnavigator

Before leading the commission that investigated the 1963 Kennedy assassination, which California governor became chief justice and authored the majority opinions in Brown v. Board of Education and Miranda v. Arizona?
Earl Warren: Chief Justice of the United States from 1953 to 1969
This Egyptian archaeologist twice served as his country's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities and has dug at sites from the Nile Delta to the Western Desert — who is he?

Its name means 'unlike other shrimp.' Known best from the Burgess Shale, this extinct radiodont swam with body flaps and stared out through huge compound eyes packed with lenses — what was this stem-arthropod?

Anomalocaris (from Ancient Greek, meaning "anomalous", and, meaning "shrimp", with the intended meaning "unlike other shrimp") is an extinct genus of radiodont, an order of early-diverging stem-group marine arthropods.
Serving King Roger II in Norman Sicily, this Arab geographer created the Tabula Rogeriana, one of the most advanced world maps of the medieval era — who was he?
Abû abd ʻAllâh Mohammad ʻibn Mohammad ʻibn ʻIdris,

These simple-looking marine invertebrates surprise biologists: their tadpole-like larvae sport a notochord and dorsal nerve cord, making them startlingly close kin to vertebrates. What are these chordates?
Tunicate: Marine animals, subphylum of chordates
A cousin of caffeine found in trace amounts in tea, coffee, and chocolate, which methylxanthine drug is used to treat asthma and COPD by blocking adenosine receptors?
Theophylline: Drug used to treat respiratory diseases
Nicknamed "Connie" and instantly recognizable by its triple tail and dolphin-shaped fuselage, which four-engined airliner was the first civil aircraft family to widely use a pressurized cabin?
Lockheed Constellation: Family of US airliners with 4 piston engines, 1943
A colorless, non-toxic gas with an octahedral, six-fluorine structure, it's over 23,000 times worse for the climate than CO2 — which hypervalent compound is it?
Sulfur hexafluoride: Chemical compound and greenhouse gas
Its dihydrate form is the mineral gypsum and its dehydrated cousin is bassanite; sparingly soluble, it causes permanent hardness in water — which inorganic salt is this?
Calcium sulfate: Chemical derived from gypsum used in food and industry
Only about 76 to 90 nucleotides long, this adaptor molecule reads each three-letter mRNA codon with a matching anticodon and ferries the right amino acid to the ribosome — what is it?
Transfer RNA: RNA that facilitates the addition of amino acids to a new protein

Defined by permanently erect fangs at the front of the mouth and ranging from a 7-inch white-lipped snake to a nearly 19-foot king, which snake family includes most of the world's neck-flaring venomous serpents?
With his booming "Hi, [name] here" and a shouted pitch, this bearded TV salesman made OxiClean a household name — who was this king of the infomercial?
Set in the fictional Pine Valley, Pennsylvania, this Agnes Nixon soap ran on ABC from 1970 to 2011 and made Susan Lucci's Erica Kane a daytime legend — what was it?
All My Children: American television soap opera

The silent one of his comedy-brother act, he never spoke on screen — communicating by horn or whistle beneath a curly reddish-blonde wig, and always playing a song on his namesake instrument. Who was he?
He co-created Spider-Man and Doctor Strange and even gave Iron Man his signature red-and-yellow look, after studying under Batman artist Jerry Robinson — who was this comic book artist?
This landlocked Southern state takes its name from the Osage language and ranges from the Ozark Mountains to the Delta lowlands along the Mississippi — which one?
Home to Australia's only active volcanoes and one of the most remote places on Earth, this sub-Antarctic territory sits 4,000 km southwest of the mainland on the Kerguelen Plateau — what is it?
Territory of Heard Island and McDonald Islands
Heard Island and McDonald Islands: External territory of Australia
Born on an Ohio farm, this hard-throwing pitcher jumped to the American League in 1901 and helped Boston win the 1903 World Series before retiring in 1911 — who was he?
Cy Young (March 29, 1867 - November 4, 1955) was an American Major League Baseball (MLB) pitcher.
Abbreviated MX and evolved from British motorcycle-trials competitions, which sport sends riders racing on enclosed off-road circuits?
Motocross: Off-road motorcycle racing held on enclosed off-road circuits
Often called Germany's most successful pop duo, this pair behind hits like "Cheri Cheri Lady" and "Brother Louie" paired producer Dieter Bohlen with singer Thomas Anders — who are they?
Produced by Ry Cooder in 1996, this ensemble of veteran Cuban musicians — some long retired — turned son and bolero into a surprise international smash. What was the group called?
Buena Vista Social Club: Cuban musical ensemble
Built on a minimal drumbeat and a famous "bass line" actually made by running a guitar through a pitch shifter, this 2003 White Stripes track became a stadium chant heard worldwide — what's its name?
Seven Nation Army: 2003 single by the White Stripes
Known for his puffed cheeks, beret, and an upward-bent trumpet, this bebop pioneer worked alongside Charlie Parker to remake modern jazz — who was he?

Born in 1990s Britain as a bright, catchy reaction against American grunge — and a cornerstone of the "Cool Britannia" moment — which guitar-pop movement put national identity front and center in its lyrics?
The middle leg of Dante's great trilogy, this canticle climbs a mountain — guided by Virgil, then Beatrice — and argues that every sin springs from love. What is it?
Purgatorio: Second part of Dante's Divine Comedy

Never once elected to office, this urban planner held myriad appointed posts over forty years and reshaped New York with his construction projects more than almost anyone in the city's history — who was he?
Unearthed in 1912 in a sculptor's Amarna workshop and now in Berlin, this painted limestone portrait of an Egyptian queen became an enduring icon of feminine beauty — what is it?
Nefertiti Bust: Ancient sculpture from Egypt

A Harvard cognitive psychologist and popular-science author, he champions evolutionary psychology and the computational theory of mind — and famously studies how children master irregular verbs. Who is he?
Dubbed the 'Prince of Preachers,' which English Particular Baptist led London's Metropolitan Tabernacle congregation for 38 years and championed the 1689 Baptist Confession?
Charles Spurgeon (19 June 1834 - 31 January 1892) was an English Particular Baptist preacher.
From a single western-Mediterranean flowering plant come both a notorious drug and the tiny dark seeds sprinkled on your bagel — which species is it?
Papaver somniferum: Species of flowering plant in the poppy family
With segmented bony armor, an upright posture, and a curling prehensile tail, these 46 species of tiny bony fish are cousins to the pipefishes and seadragons — what are they?
Seahorse (also written sea-horse and sea horse) is any of 46 species of small marine bony fish in the genus Hippocampus.
A genus of over 260 fungi, most of them parasites that bore into insects and other arthropods, this 'club-headed' organism has 1,500 years of use in Chinese medicine — what is it?
Cordyceps is a genus of ascomycete fungi (sac fungi) that includes over 260 species worldwide, many of which are parasitic.
England's very first Astronomer Royal, he compiled a 3,000-star catalogue and even spotted Uranus — though he mistakenly logged it as a star. Who was he?
John Flamsteed (19 August 1646 - 31 December 1719) was an English astronomer and the first Astronomer Royal.
Charted in 1756 by Lacaille and named for the drafting tool that draws circles, this faint southern constellation is easily confused with the mariner's-compass constellation Pyxis. Which one is it?
Circinus is a small, faint constellation in the southern sky, first defined in 1756 by the French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille.
Their foliage is almost indistinguishable from a cycad's, but flower-like reproductive organs — some likely insect-pollinated — set these common Mesozoic seed plants apart. Which extinct order?
Bennettitales (also known as cycadeoids) is an extinct order of seed plants that first appeared in the Permian period and became extinct in most areas toward the end of the Cretaceous.

Picture a spider that never learned to spin: these extinct arachnids lacked silk-producing spinnerets and wore an abdomen split into three or five distinct plates. Which order, known from the Silurian to the Permian?
Trigonotarbida is a group of extinct arachnids whose fossil record extends from the late Silurian to the early Permian (Pridoli to Sakmarian).
Sharing the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics with Martin Ryle for the discovery of pulsars, which British radio astronomer had already earned the Royal Astronomical Society's Eddington Medal in 1969?

Antony Hewish (11 May 1924 - 13 September 2021) was a British radio astronomer who won the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1974 (together with fellow radio-astronomer Martin Ryle) for his role in the discovery of pulsars.
A pioneer of women's sport, she founded the Women's World Games in the 1920s and lobbied to get more women's events into the Olympics, earning a commemorative statue in 2021 — who was she?
Alice Milliat: Pioneer of women's sport

Wisden ranked him among the four best batsmen in cricket history, and he was reckoned the finest English batsman of the 1930s — a Gloucestershire man who turned from professional to amateur and captained England. Who?
Wally Hammond (19 June 1903 - 1 July 1965) was an English first-class cricketer who played for Gloucestershire in a career that lasted from 1920 to 1951.

Jack Johnson (March 31, 1878 - June 10, 1946), nicknamed the "Galveston Giant", was an American boxer who, at the height of the Jim Crow era, became the first black world heavyweight boxing champion (1908-1915).

Classically trained before joining Miles Davis's sextet in 1958, this American jazz pianist reshaped the instrument with impressionist harmony, lush chord voicings, and "singing" melodic lines. Who was he?

Dubbed Hollywood's "angry young man" for battling executives over censorship, racism, and war, this six-time Emmy winner is best remembered for a haunting anthology series he hosted in the 1950s and '60s. Who was he?
Working undercover as a German journalist in Tokyo under the codename "Ramsay," this Soviet spy warned Moscow that Hitler planned to attack — and later that Japan would not. Who was he?
Richard Sorge: German journalist and Soviet spy (1895–1944)
A former First Amendment lawyer turned journalist, he was reporting for The Guardian in June 2013 when he began publishing a series of explosive national-security revelations. Who is he?

Forbes pegged his 1990s-into-2010s radio earnings at $84.5 million a year, and at his peak some 15.5 million listeners a week tuned into his nationally syndicated conservative talk show — which AM/FM titan was it?

This Victorian polymath wrote on everything from geology and botany to architecture and political economy, and even penned a fairy tale called The King of the Golden River — which English art critic and writer is it?

Elias Lönnrot stitched Finnish, Karelian and Ingrian folklore into one 19th-century epic — a tale of the Earth's creation and a magical wealth-making machine called the Sampo — that became the national epic of Finland; what's its name?
Kalevala: 1835 Finnish epic poem compiled by Elias Lönnrot
A creeping vine of the gourd family that originated across India, Nepal, and southern China, this plant comes in slicing, pickling, and seedless types — what is it?
Cucumber: Species of flowering plant with edible fruits
The heaviest songbird on Earth and the most widely distributed of all the corvids, this all-black passerine averages 25 inches long across the Northern Hemisphere — what is it?
Common raven: Large, black species of passerine bird
With long dense grey fur and rounded ears set oddly low on the sides of its head, this small wild cat — first described in 1776 near Lake Baikal — roams the cold steppes of Central Asia. What is it?
Pallas's cat: Species of small wild cat

The males of this Phasianidae bird are famed for piercing calls and extravagant plumage; its Asiatic species include blue, green, and a third found only in the Congo Basin — what is this bird, collectively?

Peafowl is a common name for two bird species of the genus Pavo and one species of the closely related genus Afropavo within the tribe Pavonini of the family Phasianidae (the pheasants and their allies).
Despite its name, this highly sociable oceanic dolphin earned its label from a skull resembling the orca's — it can reach 20 feet and even forms mixed pods with bottlenose dolphins. What is it?
False killer whale (Pseudorca crassidens) is a species of oceanic dolphin that is the only extant representative of the genus Pseudorca.
Fill in the blank: “____ was first called Canada between 1534 and 1763.”
study and narration of Quebec's history
History of Quebec was first called Canada between 1534 and 1763.
This Caltech chemical engineer won the 2018 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for using 'directed evolution' to engineer enzymes, and later joined Alphabet's board — who is she?
Frances Arnold (born July 25, 1956) is an American chemical engineer and Nobel Laureate.

Sharing the 1988 Nobel Prize, this American biochemist pioneered rational drug design — studying a drug's target rather than relying on trial and error — and her work led to AZT, the first widely used AIDS drug. Who was she?
Gertrude B. Elion (January 23, 1918 - February 21, 1999) was an American biochemist and pharmacologist, who shared the 1988 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with George H.

This American librarian invented a decimal classification system and helped found the American Library Association — though his legacy is marred by racism, antisemitism, and harassment of female colleagues. Who was he?
Melville Louis Kossuth "Melvil" Dewey was an American librarian and educator who invented the Dewey Decimal system of library classification.
A pioneer of investigative journalism, this Victorian editor wrote the 1885 "Maiden Tribute of Modern Babylon" series backing a law that raised the age of consent from 13 to 16. Who was he?
W. T. Stead (5 July 1849 - 15 April 1912) was an English newspaper editor who, as a pioneer of investigative journalism, became a controversial figure of the Victorian era.
Founded by an Act of Parliament in 1932, this taxpayer-funded public broadcaster carries everything from emergency alerts to entertainment across a continent — what is it?
Ignited by 2011 protests in Benghazi, this North African conflict pitted rebels and their National Transitional Council against forces loyal to Colonel Gaddafi — what was it?
Libyan civil war (2011): 2011 armed conflict in North Africa
Dubbed the "King of Gambling," this billionaire held a 40-year government monopoly over Macau's casinos and split his fortune among children who run MGM Macau and City of Dreams — who was he?
This political ideology calls for a revolutionary vanguard party to lead a "dictatorship of the proletariat" as the prelude to communism — what is it named for its Russian architect?
Leninism: Political theory developed by Vladimir Lenin
Fill in the blank: “____ is a political system, or a system of decision-making within an institution, organization, or state, in which members have a share of power.”
History of democracy is a political system, or a system of decision-making within an institution, organization, or state, in which members have a share of power.
Leader of the orthodox Sikh institution Damdami Taksal, he became the posthumous face of the Khalistan movement after Operation Bluestar in 1984 — who was he?
Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale: Figure in the Sikh Khalistan movement (1947–1984)
This Boston silversmith and engraver turned Patriot is best remembered for a 1775 midnight ride warning minutemen that British troops were on the march — who was he?
Paul Revere: American silversmith and military officer (1735–1818)
At its 14th–15th century peak this Iberian thalassocracy ruled Sicily, Sardinia, the Balearics, and even bits of Greece — born from a union of a kingdom and the County of Barcelona. What was it?
In 451 AD, a Roman-Visigothic coalition under Aetius and Theodoric I halted Attila's Huns in one of the Western Empire's last great battles — what's this clash usually called?
Battle of the Catalaunian Plains: Part of the Hunnic invasion of the Roman province of Gaul
Fought largely on Sicily and lasting 23 years, this was the longest continuous conflict and greatest naval war of antiquity — which clash between Rome and Carthage was it?
The First Punic War was the first of three wars fought between Rome and Carthage, the two main powers of the western Mediterranean in the early 3rd century BC.
A tender herb of the mint family native from Central Africa to Southeast Asia, its Genovese or 'sweet' variety is a kitchen staple worldwide — what is it?

Found only in the Americas from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego, these roughly 375 species pull off rapid, maneuverable flight thanks to an exceptional metabolism — and their males flaunt the widest plumage diversity of any bird — what are they?
He fathered the Ford Mustang in the 1960s, then rescued Chrysler from collapse as its CEO in the 1980s — one of the rare executives to run two of Detroit's Big Three. Who?
The major female sex hormone, this estrogen drives the development of secondary sexual characteristics and helps maintain reproductive tissues from puberty through pregnancy — what is it?
The most extreme form of malnutrition — a calorie deficit too deep to sustain life, sometimes wielded as a weapon and a crime under international law — goes by what name?
Starvation: Caloric intake below what is needed to maintain an organism's life
Brewed from the root of a Pacific pepper plant and sipped from a communal bowl in island ceremonies, this psychoactive drink takes its bitter-tasting name from Tongan and Marquesan — what is it?
Kava (Piper methysticum: Latin 'pepper' and Latinized Greek 'intoxicating') is a plant in the pepper family, native to the Pacific Islands.
This branch of medicine handles more than 100 inflammatory diseases of the bones, muscles, and joints — like lupus and arthritis — and overlaps heavily with immunology. What is it?
Rheumatology: Medical speciality of inflammatory diseases
One of the oldest constellations, this zodiac figure once marked the Sun's place at the spring equinox and inspired bull imagery from Sumer to Rome — which northern-sky constellation is it?
Taurus (constellation) — Taurus (Latin, 'Bull') is one of the constellations of the zodiac and is located in the northern celestial hemisphere.
More than 30,000 unsaturated hydrocarbons built on (C5H8)n units, produced mostly by plants (especially conifers) and used by some insects as defense — what class of natural compounds is this?
Terpene: Class of oily organic compounds found in plants
Once common as the refrigerant "Freon," these carbon-chlorine-fluorine compounds were phased out under the Montreal Protocol for chewing through the ozone layer — what are they?
Named for the dusky, cloud-like blotches on its coat, this Himalayan-to-Southeast-Asian wild cat uses an extraordinarily long tail to balance high in the trees — which feline is it?
The clouded leopard (Neofelis nebulosa), also called mainland clouded leopard, is a wild cat that has large dusky-grey blotches and irregular spots and stripes reminiscent of clouds.
The youngest division chief in GM history shepherded the Pontiac GTO before founding the motor company behind a stainless-steel sports car immortalized in Back to the Future — who was he?
John DeLorean: American automobile engineer and executive (1925–2005)
The first woman on Facebook's board, she turned the company profitable as its long-serving COO and founded LeanIn.Org — who is she?
Mostly made from potato starch but also found in apples and berries, this slowly-metabolized sugar alcohol is an isomer of mannitol, differing only at one hydroxyl group. What is it?
Which calculus result approximates a differentiable function near a point using a polynomial — its first-order version being the familiar linear approximation?
Taylor's theorem: Approximation of a function by a polynomial
A pioneer of radio microwave optics who also wrote science fiction and has a lunar crater named for him, this Indian polymath founded Asia's first interdisciplinary research institute — who was he?
Jagadish Chandra Bose (30 November 1858 - 23 November 1937) was an Indian polymath with interests in biology, physics and writing science fiction.

A catalyst of the New German Cinema, this prolific director made over 40 films blending Hollywood melodrama with social critique, exploring what he called 'the exploitability of feelings' — who was he?
Rainer Werner Fassbinder (31 May 1945 - 10 June 1982), sometimes credited as R.
Microsoft bundled APIs like Direct3D and DirectSound under one name, and that "X" later inspired the branding of its game console — what's this multimedia toolkit called?
DirectX: Collection of multimedia related APIs on Microsoft platforms

France's only territory in the North Pacific is an uninhabited coral atoll some 5,764 nautical miles from Paris — once called "the Rock" and worked by American guano miners in the 1890s. Which speck of land is it?
Clipperton Island: Atoll in the eastern Pacific Ocean
Established in 1395 as the first royal palace of Korea's Joseon dynasty, this Seoul landmark is where Sejong the Great oversaw the creation of the Hangul script — which palace?
Gyeongbokgung: Palace in Seoul, South Korea
A major port on India's Malabar Coast in Kerala, this city is often called Ernakulam after its central business district and anchors the state's largest metropolitan area — what is it?
He led the Green Bay Packers to five NFL titles in seven years and won the first two Super Bowls — which legendary coach, now widely ranked among the greatest in American sports?
Cricket's most successful captain ever — 220 wins — he lifted the World Cup in 2003 and 2007 and ranks third all-time in international centuries. Who is he?
Nicknamed 'Big Mac,' this slugger still holds the major-league career record for at-bats per home run, finishing with 583 homers across stints in Oakland and St. Louis — who is he?
Mark McGwire (born October 1, 1963), nicknamed "Big Mac", is an American former professional baseball first baseman.
This 1971 John Lennon anthem asks listeners to picture a world without religion, possessions, or borders — and decades later Yoko Ono finally earned a co-writing credit for it. Which song?
A Paris-born child prodigy who studied cello with his father at four, he's since won 20 Grammys recording everything from classical to bluegrass to Argentine tango — who is he?
Written by Max Martin, this 1998 debut single topped charts in over 20 countries and became one of the best-selling singles ever, with over 10 million copies sold — what teen-pop smash is it?
...Baby One More Time: 1998 single by Britney Spears
After winning a stand-up reality show in 2007, this Indian comedian built a TV empire with hit talk shows bearing his own name — who is he?
Kapil Sharma: Indian stand-up comedian and television host (born 1981)
Washington Irving wrote this 1820 tale while living in Birmingham, England, and tucked it into his collection 'The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon' — which enduring American story is it?
The Legend of Sleepy Hollow: 1820 short story by Washington Irving
He earned a physics degree before becoming a disciple of a Himalayan spiritual leader — but the world knows this title-bearing "great seer" as the man who gave us Transcendental Meditation. Who?
Nicknamed "the ornament of worshippers," this great-grandson of Muhammad survived the massacre at Karbala to become the fourth Imam in Shia Islam — who is he?
Ali al-Sajjad: Great-grandson of Muhammad and fourth Shia Imam (659–713)
Nicknamed "the King," this charismatic golfer's plain-spoken charm made him the first superstar of the sport's television age in the 1950s — who was he?
Which Sanskrit scripture — one of Hinduism's eighteen major Puranas, central to Vaishnavism — promotes devotion to Vishnu across twelve books and 18,000 verses?

By tradition the last High King of Ireland to follow the pagan inauguration rite — a symbolic marriage to the goddess of the land — and to keep the ancient Feis Temrach at Tara, who was this sixth-century ruler?
Diarmait I, High King of Ireland
Diarmait mac Cerbaill: 6th century High King of Ireland

This South Australian premier governed for over 26 years — the longest unbroken stretch of any elected leader in Australian history — and was famous for shamelessly haranguing federal leaders into funding his state. Who was he?
Thomas Playford IV: 20th-century Australian politician and fruit grower (1896–1981)

After studying in New Zealand and a stint in the Ministry of Finance, this man unseated the incumbent to become chief minister, then in 1979 became the very first president of a Pacific island nation — who is he?
Ieremia Tabai: President of Kiribati from 1979 to 1982 and 1983 to 1991
A National Hero of his country, this statesman founded Sri Lanka's first political party in 1935 and fought in both the Indian and Sri Lankan independence movements — who was he?

Eldest daughter of a Raiatean king, she became a queen consort of Tahiti through an arranged marriage to a widowed second cousin, then ruled as Queen of Huahine — and even fought in the Battle of Te Feipī. Who was she?
Teriitaria II: Queen of Tahiti and Huahine (c. 1790 – 1858)
Twice elected mayor of Washington D.C., this Whig newspaperman amassed one of the most extensive private collections of Revolutionary-era maps and manuscripts in America — who was he?
Peter Force: American politician and historian (1790–1868)

The type species that gives its name to the Oleaceae family of lilac, jasmine, and ash, this Mediterranean evergreen bears a fruit classed botanically as a drupe — like a cherry or peach — what is it?
First domesticated in Mesoamerica and led in production today by India, this tropical fruit belongs to the small genus Carica — what is it?
Papaya: Species of tropical fruit plant
Native to Central Asia and a close relative of the onion, shallot, and leek, this bulbous Allium has been a seasoning and folk remedy known to Babylonians, Egyptians, and Romans alike — what is it?

This genus of 700-plus flowering trees gets its name from Greek words meaning 'well covered' — a nod to the little cap fused over its stamens — and most species are native to Australia. The leafy 'gum trees' in question are which?
Eucalyptus is a genus of more than 700 species of flowering plants in the family Myrtaceae.
This extinct archaic human was the first to evolve a humanlike body and gait, the first to leave Africa for Asia and Europe, and the first to wield fire — who were they?
Homo erectus: Extinct species of archaic human
Making up just 1% of described fungal species, these single-celled eukaryotes reproduce by budding or fission and usually measure a mere 3–4 micrometers across — what are they?
Yeast is any species of fungus that grows primarily in a unicellular form and reproduces via budding or fission.
An economist who entered parliament via a 1981 by-election, this Samoan politician went on to serve as his country's prime minister from 1998 all the way to 2021 — who is he?
Tuilaʻepa Saʻilele Malielegaoi: Prime Minister of Samoa from 1998 to 2021
Born in 1847, this American wore three hats at once — psychologist, logician, and mathematician. Who was she?
Christine Ladd-Franklin (December 1, 1847 - March 5, 1930) was an American psychologist, logician, and mathematician.

A trained civil engineer who oversaw concerts at the Crystal Palace, this Englishman's program notes grew into a famous music dictionary — and he once hunted Vienna for lost Schubert manuscripts with Arthur Sullivan. Who was he?
George Grove: English engineer and writer on music (1820–1900)
Born in 1863, this Italian is remembered as a major contributor to the early development of algebraic geometry — who was he?
This Eastern Han hydrologist is credited as the first to harness a waterwheel to power the bellows of a blast furnace for forging cast iron — who was this ingenious engineer?
Du Shi: 1st-century engineer, metallurgist and politician
Born in 1869 into an old Anglo-Irish scientific family in Dublin, she is considered the world's first woman medical physicist — who was she?
Edith Anne Stoney: Anglo-Irish medical physicist
This Hungarian nuclear chemist became the world's leading expert in isotope separation and polonium preparation, and confirmed the existence of "Uranium-Y" — who was she?
Hailed as 'the Emperor of Rasa-Abhinaya,' this 20th-century Kerala performer and Sanskrit scholar was famed for his eye-driven acting in the ancient Koodiyattam theatre tradition. Who was he?

Widely considered the most important filmmaker of early Korean cinema — and possibly Korea's first true movie star — he wrote, directed, and acted in his own films, founding the country's auteur tradition. Who was he?
Na Un'gyu: Korean filmmaker and actor (1902–1937)
This Irish-Canadian defenceman won gold at the first seven Women's World Championships and saw her number 91 retired by the Toronto Aeros — which hockey great is it?
Geraldine Heaney: Irish-Canadian ice hockey player and coach (born 1967)

He founded the original Kingston Frontenacs, refereed and coached in the early Ontario Hockey Association, and was instrumental in creating the 1919 Memorial Cup — which Canadian "founding father" of the sport spread it across the country?
James T. Sutherland (October 10, 1870 - September 16, 1955) was a Canadian ice hockey administrator, and founding father of the game in Canada.

Acclaimed for her Wagner and Strauss heroines, this French soprano later reinvented herself in mezzo roles when vocal troubles arrived in the early 1970s — prized throughout for the warmth and subtlety of her singing. Who was she?

Formed in 1964, this South African female group fronted by soprano Hilda Tloubatla blended girl-group harmonies and high-energy choreography into mbaqanga, offering joyful respite during apartheid — which group is it?
Mahotella Queens: South African female band
Befriended by Mozart and Paisiello, who wrote roles for him, this Irish tenor became so famous in Italy that locals called him "Signor Ochelli" — which singer was he?
Michael Kelly was an Irish tenor, composer and theatrical manager who made an international career of importance in musical history.
Crowned the "King of Salegy," this Malagasy singer dragged an obscure northwestern regional style into national and international fame and even spun off two subgenres of his own — who is he?
Eusèbe Jaojoby: Composer and singer from Madagascar
Said to have had the longest and most versatile vocal career history records, this Victorian-era baritone debuted in Italy in 1857 before basing himself in England for life — who was he?

Born from the 2024 merger of Cedar Fair and a famous flag-themed chain, this Charlotte-based company is North America's largest regional amusement park operator, hosting over 50 million guests a year — what is it?
Six Flags: American amusement park company
His 1839 compendium American Slavery as It Is partly inspired Uncle Tom's Cabin and is ranked second only to it in shaping the antislavery cause — which abolitionist architect?

Theodore Dwight Weld (November 23, 1803 - February 3, 1895) was one of the architects of the American abolitionist movement during its formative years from 1830 to 1844, playing a role as writer, editor, speaker, and organizer.

Inspired by Thomas Carlyle, this English historian abandoned a planned clerical career after his scandalous 1849 novel 'The Nemesis of Faith' and went on to write a sweeping 'History of England' — who was he?
James Anthony Froude: English historian, novelist and biographer (1818–1894)

A Chinese writer and archaeologist who co-founded the Literary Study Society and edited 'Fiction Monthly,' he also became the very first director of the Palace Museum in the Forbidden City — who was he?
A French rationalist and scourge of the Catholic Church, this author was a close friend of Voltaire who spent much of his life in exile at the court of Frederick the Great — who was he?
Jean-Baptiste de Boyer, Marquis d'Argens: French philosopher and writer (1704–1771)
A dharma-heir of Xuefeng Yicun, this Tang-dynasty Chan master lent his name to one of Zen's five major schools and inspired the later Blue Cliff Record — who was he?
Yunmen Wenyan (862 or 864 - 949 CE), was a major Chinese Chan master of the Tang dynasty.

Appointed Poet Laureate in 1896 — reputedly as a reward for backing Lord Salisbury's Conservatives — this Englishman was so mocked that a contemporary marveled his verse could be 'such poor stuff' while he imagined it immortal. Who was he?
A German theologian who had converted from Judaism, he preached against the Jews, tried to destroy copies of the Talmud, and waged a long pamphlet war with the humanist Johann Reuchlin — who was he?
A musician, poet, and politician of the Northern Song dynasty from Qiantang, he went by the art name Qingzhen Jushi and left behind a poetry anthology bearing the same name — who was he?

Hailed by some as 'Japan's greatest lacquerer,' this late-Edo and early-Meiji painter and print artist was viewed back home as both too Westernized and too conservative, yet became a darling of collectors in Britain and America — who was he?

Seamus Heaney credited this Raasay-raised poet with single-handedly saving Scottish Gaelic verse, after he traded a strict Presbyterian upbringing for socialism and friendships with the Scottish Renaissance — who was he?

The highest-paid magazine writer of his day, this American worked alongside Poe and Longfellow — and even employed Harriet Jacobs as a children's nurse while she wrote her own autobiography. Who was he?
Nathaniel Parker Willis: American magazine writer, editor, and publisher (1806–1867)

This American critic championed 'close reading' — what she called reading from a writer's point of view — and turned that lens on everyone from Shakespeare to Seamus Heaney in the pages of The New Yorker. Who was she?
Helen Vendler (ne Hennessy; April 30, 1933 - April 23, 2024) was an American academic, writer and literary critic.

One of Oceania's most influential writers, this Samoan poet who lives in New Zealand wrote 'Sons for the Return Home' and 'Leaves of the Banyan Tree' and won the Commonwealth Writers Prize twice — who is he?
Albert Wendt: Samoan poet and writer

One of North Korea's most important fiction writers, he headed the Korean Writers' Union and served as Minister of Education, even helping drive the very purges that swept up his rival writers. Who was he?

Eulogized as the 'Grand Old Woman of Australia,' this Scottish-born writer and reformer became Australia's first female political candidate in 1897 and also preached at an Adelaide Unitarian church. Who was she?
Catherine Helen Spence: Australian writer, preacher, and reformer (1825–1910)

Rejected for a university post in 1956 because few locals then held academic jobs, this poet spent nine years in the civil service before rising to full professor and becoming a pioneer of English literature in his island nation. Who is he?
Edwin Thumboo: Singaporean poet and academic (born 1933)

Queen Victoria's favorite poet and, per Coventry Patmore, the most popular of her day after Tennyson, this Englishwoman published in Dickens's periodicals and wrote of homelessness, poverty, and 'fallen women.' Who was she?
Adelaide Anne Procter: English poet and philanthropist (1825–1864)
This poet of the Liu Song dynasty is best remembered for his 'Fu on the Ruined City,' a long rhapsody mourning the wreck of Guangling, today's Yangzhou. Who was he?
Bao Zhao: Chinese poet and official

A painter, composer, and translator who earned his short nickname from fellow art students, this writer is one of Madagascar's most important literary figures, his works taught at every grade level since 1960. Who is he?

Billed as 'the most successful female playwright of the eighteenth century,' her stage pieces kept being performed long after rivals were forgotten, earning her the title of second woman of the English stage after Aphra Behn. Who was she?
Susanna Centlivre: English actor and writer (c. 1669 – 1723)

A 'legendary figure in Chinese art and literary circles,' he wrote over 40 plays and scripts — including his masterpiece 'Return on a Snowy Night' — and directed Hong Kong's first colour film, while openly criticizing China's cultural policies. Who was he?
Dubbed 'Korea's Mayakovsky' and later 'the Pushkin of Korea,' this Soviet-born poet is hailed as the founding father of North Korean poetry for his lyrical epic, socialist-realist style. Who was he?
Known mostly through two poems by Martial, this ancient Roman poet wrote frankly sensual love poetry about her desire for her husband during Domitian's reign — who was she?
Sulpicia (satirist) — Sulpicia was an ancient Roman poet who was active during the reign of the emperor Domitian (r.
A multilingual painter, sculptor, printmaker, and raconteur, he has been described as Zambia's most famous painter. Who was he?
Henry Tayali: Zambian artist, sculptor, printmaker, and lecturer (1943–1987)
A first-generation Polish American avant-garde artist who calls her aesthetic 'American futurism,' she's credited with coining the very term 'performance poetry' back in 1979 — who is she?

Hedwig Gorski (born July 18, 1949) is an American performance poet and an avant-garde artist who labels her aesthetic as "American futurism." The term "performance poetry," a precursor to slam poetry, is attributed to her.

Imprisoned for ten years and tortured until he could no longer walk, this Syrian journalist and dissident kept criticizing his government's human rights abuses from a Mezzeh isolation cell — who is he?
Nizar Nayyouf (also Nayuf or Nayouf;; born 29 May 1962) is a Syrian journalist, human rights activist, and dissident.
A wealthy Georgia medical doctor who turned to verse, he's best remembered for his friendship with Edgar Allan Poe and his fierce defense of the poet after Poe's death — who was he?
Thomas Holley Chivers (October 18, 1809 - December 18, 1858) was an American medical doctor-turned-poet from the state of Georgia.
An influential 19th-century Lebanese painter who trained in Rome and once painted a portrait of Pope Pius IX, he also mentored a young Khalil Gibran. Who was he?

Celticists credit this 19th-century poet and folklorist with preserving an immense trove of legends for the Isle of Man; he's considered the last important first-language writer of his endangered Manx tongue. Who was he?

Taking her pen name from a Mississippi river near her home, this American poet inherited the New Orleans Daily Picayune from her late husband and became the first female editor of a major American newspaper. Who was she?
Pearl Rivers: American poet and journalist

Hailed as the "dean of black dramatists," this Black Chicago Renaissance playwright swept the spiritual ballads and feverish dancing out of "Negro theatricals" in favor of naturalistic plots and characters drawn from Depression-era urban life — who was he?

This English inventor pioneered the salted-paper and calotype photographic processes and published "The Pencil of Nature," one of the first books illustrated with photographs. Who was this photography pioneer?
Henry Fox Talbot: English photography pioneer (1800–1877)
Before he became the first governor of New South Wales, this British naval officer started out as an apprentice on a whaling ship and even spent time seconded to the Portuguese Navy — who was he?
Arthur Phillip (11 October 1738 - 31 August 1814) was a British Royal Navy officer who served as the first governor of the Colony of New South Wales.
This Royal Navy navigator led the first inshore circumnavigation of mainland Australia and championed the very name "Australia" as "more agreeable to the ear." Who was he?

Matthew Flinders (16 March 1774 - 19 July 1814) was an English Royal Navy officer, navigator and cartographer who led the first inshore circumnavigation of mainland Australia, then called New Holland.
Commissioned by a judge's Transylvania Company in 1775, this frontiersman blazed the Wilderness Road through the Cumberland Gap and founded Boonesborough — which early American folk hero?
Left for dead by his companions after a grizzly mauling on the Upper Missouri, this frontiersman's survival inspired the films Man in the Wilderness and The Revenant — who was he?
Hugh Glass: American fur trapper and frontiersman (1783–1833)
On Interpol's top-10 most-wanted list for robberies in the 1970s and '80s, this Serbian warlord later led the feared Serb Volunteer Guard through the Yugoslav Wars — by what single name was he known?
Arkan: Serbian paramilitary commander and mobster (1952–2000)
Traditionally said to have been founded in 843, this sovereign state occupied the northern third of Great Britain and fought England in the Wars of Independence — what was it?
Kingdom of Scotland: Sovereign state in Europe (843–1707)
Born of the 1978 Saur Revolution and leaning so heavily on Soviet aid it was widely called a Soviet satellite, this left-wing state lasted until 1992 — what was it?
Democratic Republic of Afghanistan: Afghan state from 1978 to 1992

This American naval aviator and polar explorer discovered Mount Sidley — Antarctica's largest dormant volcano — and claimed to be first to reach both Poles by air, though the North Pole claim remains disputed. Who was he?
Rear Admiral Richard E. Byrd, Jr.
Richard E. Byrd: American naval officer (1888–1957)
He began his career studying geology in Gansu before rising to become Premier of China from 2003 to 2013 — which retired Communist Party leader?
Wen Jiabao: Premier of China from 2003 to 2013

Starting from stem cells near the wall of the seminiferous tubules, this multi-stage process runs cells through two rounds of meiosis to turn diploid germ cells into haploid swimmers. What is it called?
A volatile, colorless liquid with a sweet, chloroform-like smell, this organochlorine (formula CH2Cl2) is slightly polar, won't mix with water, and is prized as a widely-used solvent. What is it?
Fill in the blank: “____ (Varanus salvator) is a large varanid lizard native to South and Southeast Asia.”
Asian water monitor (Varanus salvator) is a large varanid lizard native to South and Southeast Asia.
Every snake in this venomous family wields unusually long, hinged fangs for deep envenomation — and many give live birth, a trait echoed in their Latin-rooted name. What snakes are these?
Also called vitamin B2, this nutrient forms two key coenzymes for energy metabolism, can be prescribed for corneal thinning, and taken orally may cut down migraines in adults — which vitamin is it?
Riboflavin: Vitamin, dietary supplement, and yellow food dye
Caused by abnormalities in the genome — a single faulty gene, multiple genes, or a chromosome glitch, inherited or arising de novo — what is the general medical term for this kind of health problem?
Genetic disorder: Health problem from genome abnormalities
Its name comes from Greek for 'milk flower,' and this small genus of about 20 bulbous perennials nods with a single white bell of six tepals — what is the botanical name for the snowdrop?
Galanthus (from Ancient Greek, (gla, "milk") + (nthos, "flower")), or snowdrop, is a small genus of approximately 20 species of bulbous perennial herbaceous plants in the family Amaryllidaceae.
One of the three great clades of dinosaur, its members share hollow bones and three clawed toes per limb, were ancestrally carnivorous, and likely wore feathers in the Coelurosauria — which group?
In this learning process, voluntary behaviors are shaped by their consequences — strengthened by reinforcement, weakened by punishment or extinction. What is it called?
Operant conditioning: Type of associative learning process for behavioral modification

An Atlanta factory superintendent with a Cornell engineering degree, he was wrongly convicted of murdering a young employee, then kidnapped from prison and lynched — a case that became a focus of antisemitism. Who was he?
Medically termed a 'spontaneous abortion,' this is the loss of an embryo or fetus before it can survive independently — distinct from a stillbirth, which occurs after 20 weeks. What is it?
Miscarriage: Natural premature termination of pregnancy
Fill in the blank: “____ (Myrmecophaga tridactyla) is an insectivorous mammal native to Central and South America.”
Giant anteater (Myrmecophaga tridactyla) is an insectivorous mammal native to Central and South America.
This waxy crystalline compound from peppermint and corn mint produces a cooling sensation when inhaled or rubbed on skin, and brings local-anesthetic relief to a sore throat — what is it?
Menthol: Organic compound used as flavouring and analgesic
The sole surviving family of an ancient cephalopod lineage, these nine living species carry coiled chambered shells 10 to 25 cm across and are all protected under CITES — what creatures are they?
Black-and-yellow social wasps that live in colonies and do a rapid side-to-side wiggle just before landing go by what North American common name?
Yellowjacket: Common name for two genera of wasps
Made in the adrenal cortex, this hormone tells the kidney to hang onto sodium and dump potassium, quietly steering your blood pressure and blood volume — what is it?
Its severe chronic form, beriberi, may take its name from a Sinhalese phrase meaning 'I cannot, I cannot' — what vitamin B1 shortfall causes it?
Thiamine deficiency is a medical condition of low levels of thiamine (vitamin B1).

A former Goldman Sachs banker who once ran the Biosphere 2 research project and chaired Breitbart News, this strategist lasted seven months as a President's chief strategist before being fired — who is he?
Steve Bannon: American media executive and political strategist (born 1953)
Centered on the upper-middle-class Huxtables of Brooklyn and spawning the spin-off A Different World, this NBC sitcom drew on its star's stand-up routines about family life — what was it?
The Cosby Show: American television sitcom (1984–1992)
Set among the market traders of working-class Peckham, this John Sullivan sitcom followed half-brothers Del Boy and Rodney Trotter scheming to get rich — which BBC comedy was it?
Only Fools and Horses: British television sitcom (1981–2003)

Curiously, this glittering 4.2-mile stretch of casinos and resorts sits not in the city it's named for, but just south of its limits in the unincorporated towns of Paradise and Winchester — what is it?
The Las Vegas Strip is a stretch of Las Vegas Boulevard in Clark County, Nevada, that is known for its concentration of resort hotels and casinos.

Named for a nearby modern village along the old course of the Ravi River, this ancient Pakistani Punjab city of up to 23,500 people was badly damaged when the British carted off its bricks for railway ballast — what site is it?
Harappa: Archaeological site in Punjab, Pakistan
Fill in the blank: “____ is a 630-foot-tall (192 m) monument in St.”
Gateway Arch is a 630-foot-tall (192 m) monument in St.

Once the ducal seat of Lorraine after a fortified town was founded here in the 11th century, this city on the left bank of the Meurthe is now the largest urban area in its region — which French city is it?
Nancy, France is the prefecture of the northeastern French department of Meurthe-et-Moselle, located in the Grand Est region (in the historical region of Lorraine).
Descended from samurai swordsmanship, this modern Japanese martial art is fought with bamboo swords and protective armor — its name literally means 'way of the sword.' What is it?
Nicknamed 'the Left Arm of God,' this Dodgers ace was the first three-time Cy Young winner before chronic elbow pain forced him to retire at just 30 — who was he?
Sandy Koufax (n Braun; born December 30, 1935), nicknamed "the Left Arm of God", is an American former professional baseball player.
The NFL's all-time leading rusher spent most of his 15 seasons with the Dallas Cowboys after starring for the Florida Gators — which running back?
Emmitt Smith (born May 15, 1969) is an American former professional football running back who played in the National Football League (NFL) for 15 seasons, primarily with the Dallas Cowboys.
A two-time Olympic 100m champion and five-time world champion, this Jamaican sprinter helped usher in her island's golden age of speed over a career spanning a decade and a half — who is she?
Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce: Retired Jamaican track and field sprinter (born 1986)
Spanish duo Los del Río first recorded this song in 1993, but a Bayside Boys remix with added English lyrics turned it into a 14-week US No. 1 and a dance craze — what is it?
Macarena: 1993 single by Los del Río
Founded in 1851 in Rochester, New York, this company dominated American telegraphy for over a century and pioneered wire money transfers alongside its telegram business — what is it?
Western Union is an American multinational financial services corporation headquartered in Denver, Colorado.

Born into a fallen aristocratic family in Saint Petersburg, this Bolshevik theorist embraced Marxism, was exiled to Siberia alongside the man she'd marry, and became a leading figure in the party — who was she?
Nadezhda Krupskaya: Wife of Vladimir Lenin (1869–1939)

Verdi composed this 1841 opera, whose four-act libretto by Temistocle Solera draws on the biblical books of Kings, Jeremiah and Daniel, premiering at La Scala — what is its short title, drawn from a Babylonian king's name?
Encouraged by Louis Leakey, this American primatologist studied mountain gorillas daily in Rwanda's forests and wrote "Gorillas in the Mist" before her 1985 murder — who was she?

Lancashire-born and West Coast-settled, this Liberal politician became New Zealand's longest-serving head of government, holding the premiership for thirteen years until his death in 1906 — who was he?
Richard Seddon: Prime minister of New Zealand from 1893 to 1906

From at least the early 15th century to the mid-1800s, this Chewa polity led by the Kalonga controlled what is now central and southern Malawi plus parts of Mozambique and Zambia — what was this empire?
Maravi: Former empire which straddled the current borders of Malawi, Mozambique, and Zambia

A former major under dictator Jorge Ubico, this Guatemalan officer became one of three junta members guiding the country toward democracy in 1944, even as he balked at letting the elected president take office — who was he?
Francisco Javier Arana: Guatemalan military leader (1905–1949)

This German-American newspaper editor and orator popularized 'propaganda of the deed' in the United States and was jailed several times after publishing literature on how to build and use bombs — who was he?
Johann Most (February 5, 1846 - March 17, 1906) was a German-American Social Democratic and then anarchist politician, newspaper editor, and orator.

The longest-serving prime minister of Iceland and former mayor of Reykjavík, he later chaired the Central Bank — and the 2008 financial crisis sparked loud public demands for his resignation. Who was he?

An explorer, lawyer and one of colonial New South Wales' wealthiest figures, he co-founded Australia's first independent newspaper and championed emancipists, trial by jury and self-government — who was he?
William Wentworth: Australian statesman, writer and explorer

Exiled to Argos at age seven after his father was killed in a coup, this Hellenistic Greek later freed his home city from tyranny and was elected strategos of the Achaean League seventeen times — who was he?
Aratus of Sicyon: Greek statesman and general (271–213 BCE)

As president of the Royal Geographical Society, this English explorer organized the British National Antarctic Expedition of 1901–04 and personally launched the polar career of Robert Falcon Scott. Who was he?
Clements Markham (20 July 1830 - 30 January 1916) was an English geographer, explorer and writer.
Smaller and shorter-necked than their swan and goose cousins in the family Anatidae, these aquatic birds are often confused with grebes, loons, and coots — what are they?
Duck: Common name for many species of bird

With over 2,400 species sporting triangular heads, bulging eyes on flexible necks, and folded forelegs built to snatch prey, these insects count termites and cockroaches among their closest relatives — what are they?
Mantis are an order (Mantodea) of insects that contains over 2,400 species in about 460 genera in 33 families.
This English clergyman was the first person ever to measure blood pressure, and on the side he invented a ventilator and even wrote a tract against drinking — who was he?
Stephen Hales: English clergyman and scientist (1677–1761)

A Belgian-British emigrant to New York, this inventor struck gold during a 1906 stay in Central America by perfecting an early instant-coffee process and building a company to mass-produce it — who was he?
George Constant Louis Washington[I] was a Belgian-British inventor and businessman.

This Italian-American physicist invented an improved coincidence circuit and traveled to Eritrea to prove cosmic rays arrive more strongly from the West than the East, before Italy's racial laws forced him to flee — who was he?
A Scottish surgeon who corrected clubfoot and squints, he's also dubbed by some the 'Father of Modern Hypnotism' — pioneering both hypnotic and chemical anaesthesia. Who was this gentleman scientist?

James Braid was a Scottish surgeon, natural philosopher, and "gentleman scientist". He was a significant innovator in the treatment of clubfoot, spinal curvature, knock-knees, bandy legs, and squint; a significant pioneer of hypnotism and hypnotherapy, and an important and influential pioneer in the adoption of both hypnotic anaesthesia and chemical anaesthesia.
He is regarded by some, such as William S. Kroger (2008, p. 3), as the "Father of Modern Hypnotism".
This American physicist won the 1989 Nobel for inventing the separated oscillatory field method behind atomic clocks, and helped found both Brookhaven National Laboratory and Fermilab — who was he?
While awaiting a US visa in a Vichy France internment camp, this future rabbi met the man who'd become the seventh Chabad Rebbe — and went on to co-found the Jewish Renewal movement. Who was he?
Zalman Schachter-Shalomi: American Rabbi, writer, and activist
The only Saskatchewan-born Nobel laureate, this Canadian-born chemist won the 1983 prize for unraveling the mechanisms of electron-transfer reactions in metal complexes — who was he?

A pioneer of modern control theory whose collaboration with Claude Shannon helped lay the foundations of the Information Age, he also helped design the automatic guns that defended London from V-1 flying bombs — who was he?
Hendrik Wade Bode: American scientist and engineer (1905–1982)
