This English novelist is best known for "A Dance to the Music of Time," a 12-volume saga published over nearly a quarter century that ranks among the longest novels in English. Who was he?

An English author and poet who married twice while working as a translator at Bletchley Park during WWII, she's better remembered for being initiated in 1953 into the tradition of Gardnerian Wicca and writing much of its early liturgy — who is she?

Born in the Russian Empire and raised speaking Yiddish at home, this American artist abandoned painting and printing to build her lifework from found objects — monumental, monochromatic wooden wall pieces. Who is she?
This American gossip columnist and professional hostess is credited with introducing the scavenger hunt as a modern party game, and threw legendary bashes for royalty and high society — who was she?
Elsa Maxwell: American gossip columnist and author (1883–1963)
In this 1847 Balzac novel, an unmarried middle-aged woman teams up with a discontented young wife to seduce and ruin the men of her own extended family — part of his Human Comedy. What's the book?
Cousin Bette: 1847 novel by Honoré de Balzac
A student of G.S. Ghurye and a writer from Maharashtra, she is regarded as the first female Indian sociologist — who was she?
Irawati Karve: Indian sociologist and writer (1905–1970)

Named in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad as a wife of the sage Yajnavalkya, this Vedic-era thinker probed the nature of the soul in a famous dialogue and is remembered as an expounder of the Veda — who was she?
Maitreyi: Vedic philosopher from ancient India

This Greek poet turned a lost astronomy treatise into a hugely popular hexameter poem about the constellations and the weather — beloved across the Greek and Roman world despite his own shaky grasp of astronomy. Who was he?
This 1936 Kaufman-and-Hart comedy in three acts won the 1937 Pulitzer for Drama and remains one of the most-produced school plays year after year. Which play is it?
You Can't Take It with You
You Can't Take It with You (play)
You Can't Take It with You
You Can't Take It with You is a comedic play in three acts by George S. Kaufman and Moss Hart.
You Can't Take It with You (play)

This American philosopher of mind laid the groundwork for the "modularity of mind" and the "language of thought" hypotheses, and was called hugely influential across nearly all philosophy of mind since 1960 — who was he?

Time called her the "literary godmother" to Paris's Lost Generation, and her Black Sun Press printed early Hemingway and Henry Miller — but she also patented the first successful modern bra. Who was she?
The first Laureate for Irish Fiction, this writer won the 2007 Man Booker Prize for her novel The Gathering and explores family, love, and motherhood in her work — who is she?

This prolific English author published several books a year, using a different pen name for each genre — Jean Plaidy for royal history, Victoria Holt for gothic romance, Philippa Carr for family sagas. What was her birth name?
This American modernist poet, also a critic, translator, and editor, was prized for her formal innovation, precise diction, irony, and wit — who was she?
This Manchester-born English novelist trained as a lawyer but won fame in 1834 with Rookwood, which made the highwayman Dick Turpin its leading character — who was he?

This English journalist is forever tied to her 1861 Book of Household Management, though she'd cheerfully plagiarised the recipes for her husband's magazine from other works — who was she, better known by her married title?
Isabella Beeton: English journalist, publisher and writer (1836–1865)

Born into extreme poverty in Michigan and taught to read and write by herself, this convent-educated woman turned anti-authoritarian and became an American anarchist feminist writer and speaker — who was she?
Voltairine de Cleyre: American anarchist writer and feminist (1866–1912)
Born into Malay aristocracy in North Sumatra and recalled home in 1937 to marry a sultan's daughter, this poet became a National Hero of Indonesia — who was he?
This Puerto Rican poet and teacher was also a fierce independence advocate, serving as Secretary General of the women's branch of the Nationalist Party — who was she?
Julia de Burgos: Puerto Rican poet (1914–1953)
Dublin-born and New York-raised, this Beaux-Arts sculptor won acclaim for Civil War monuments like the Robert Gould Shaw Memorial on Boston Common and his Abraham Lincoln: The Man — who was he?
Augustus Saint-Gaudens: American sculptor and engraver (1848–1907)

This German-American psychiatrist treated poor Black patients at his Lafargue Clinic, and his findings on institutional stress were cited in Brown v. Board of Education — yet he's best remembered for crusading against the supposed harms of comic books. Who was he?
Fredric Wertham (born Friedrich Ignatz Wertheimer) was a German-American psychiatrist and author.

A general, poet, and inventor of the Song dynasty, this commander was famed for winning battles against larger forces — and was said to have ended his career covered in scars with only four fingers left on his hands. Who was he?
Born in 1655, this Italian instrument maker earned lasting fame for inventing a keyboard instrument that could play both soft and loud — who was he?
Bartolomeo Cristofori (Italian; May 4, 1655 - January 27, 1731) was an Italian maker of musical instruments famous for inventing the piano.
A French revolutionary journalist who, in 'The Tribune of the People,' called for revolt against the Directory and championed the abolition of private property — who is this proto-communist?
François-Noël Babeuf: French revolutionary and journalist (1760–1797)

Married to the fourth U.S. president, she pioneered bipartisan socializing by hosting Washington functions for both parties — a sharp break from one-party-at-a-time predecessors like Jefferson; who is she?
Dolley Madison: First Lady of the United States from 1809 to 1817
Introduced to Hitler by Dietrich Eckart, this Baltic German edited the Völkischer Beobachter and ran the Nazi bureau for cultural policy and surveillance that bore his own name — who was he?
A 14th-century Italian mystic who waded into papal politics through relentless letter-writing, she was later named a Doctor of the Church — which saint was she?

Caterina di Jacopo di Benincasa, TOSD, known as Catherine of Siena, was an Italian Catholic mystic and diplomat who engaged in papal and Italian politics through extensive letter-writing and advocacy.
Rooted in the now-discredited doctrine of scientific racism, this belief served as a key justification for European colonialism and the Atlantic slave trade — what is it called?
White supremacy is the belief that white people are superior to those of other races.
Before becoming the Supreme Court's first African-American justice, he argued 32 civil rights cases before it and won 29 — culminating in the landmark Brown v. Board of Education. Who was he?
Thurgood Marshall: US Supreme Court justice from 1967 to 1991

This Dominican friar prophesied civic glory for Renaissance Florence and called for the destruction of secular art — his predictions seeming to come true when Charles VIII of France invaded Italy in 1494. Who was he?
Girolamo Savonarola: De facto ruler of Florence from 1494 to 1498; Dominican friar and reformer

On a single 1929 day in a Chicago garage, seven men were lined against a wall and gunned down — some of the killers disguised as police — in a brutal flashpoint of Prohibition-era gang warfare. What is this killing known as?
Saint Valentine's Day Massacre: 1929 gang shooting in Chicago

In her teens this Lemhi Shoshone woman traveled thousands of miles from North Dakota to the Pacific with an expedition exploring the Louisiana Territory, later embraced as a suffrage-era symbol of women's worth — who is she?
Sacagawea (or s-; also spelled Sakakawea or Sacajawea; c.
Found naturally in mammals' milk and a direct precursor to phenethylamine, this is one of nine amino acids your body can't make, so you eat it in meat, eggs, and legumes — which one?
Sold as Versed, this benzodiazepine sedates rather than knocks you out, can be sprayed up the nose or squirted in the cheek, and famously causes anterograde amnesia — which drug?
Midazolam: Benzodiazepine used for anesthesia and procedural sedation

Exercise, laughter, dancing, and romantic love can all trigger this intense state of well-being via the brain's pleasure centers — though it's also a symptom of mania and the lure of addictive drugs. What is it?

Believed to be an autoimmune attack on the immune privilege of hair follicles, this condition typically leaves a few coin-sized bald spots — and in rare cases takes every hair on the body. What's it called?
Made by grinding dry-roasted legumes and often tweaked with salt or emulsifiers, this protein-rich spread is the most popular of all the nut butters — what is it?
Peanut butter is a food paste or spread made from ground, dry-roasted peanuts.
Battered and fried, this 19th-century English dish was so cherished that the British government safeguarded its supply through both World Wars — what is it?
Fish and chips is a hot dish consisting of battered and fried fish, served with chips.
Whose name comes from Greek words for 'congealed' and 'curdled' — this plant-cell-wall polymer is extracted from citrus as a powder that makes jams and jellies set?
Pectin: Structural carbohydrate in the cell walls of land plants and some algae
The average adult sheds 50 to 70 billion cells a day through this tidy, programmed cell death — named from a Greek word for 'falling off' — quite unlike messy, traumatic necrosis. What is it?
Apoptosis: Form of programmed cell death
Often called eczema, this umbrella term covers skin inflammation marked by itchiness, redness, and a rash, sometimes with small blisters or thickened skin — what is it?
Dermatitis is a term used for different types of skin inflammation, typically characterized by itchiness, redness and a rash.
Also called the woodchuck, this North American rodent is exceptional among its kin: while most marmots live in rocky mountains, this lowland burrower roams the Eastern U.S. into Alaska — what is it?
Groundhog (Marmota monax), also known as the woodchuck, is a rodent of the family Sciuridae, belonging to the group of large ground squirrels known as marmots.
Taken by mouth, smeared as a cream, or injected, this antiviral medication is a frontline treatment for herpes simplex, chickenpox, and shingles. What is it?
Aciclovir: Antiviral medication used against herpes, chickenpox, and shingles
This white solid is prized for binding iron and calcium ions into water-soluble complexes — handy for dissolving scale — and goes by a four-letter acronym. What is it?
Native to East Asia but a notorious invasive pest in Europe and North America, this knotweed has won over beekeepers and foragers alike, its young stems tasting of lemony rhubarb. What plant is it?

Found across Africa, Asia, and Australia, this family of nonvenomous snakes — including some of the world's largest — must coil around prey and squeeze it into cardiac arrest before swallowing it whole. What is the family?

Named after a colourful terrestrial flower, this predatory marine cnidarian is typically a single polyp anchored to a hard surface — a tentacled relative of coral and jellyfish, but with no medusa stage. What is it?
Sea anemone: Marine animals of the order Actiniaria
First published in 1876 as a mere 44-page pamphlet, this library system organizes books by discipline and subject and is now maintained by OCLC — what is it?
The Dewey Decimal Classification, colloquially known as the Dewey Decimal System, is a proprietary library classification system which organizes books based on discipline and subject.
Set in the fictional city of Port Charles and on the air since 1963, this ABC daytime drama began as a half-hour serial before expanding to a full hour. What is it?
General Hospital: American television soap opera (since 1963)
Created by Sherwood Schwartz, this CBS sitcom of the mid-1960s followed seven mismatched castaways whose escape attempts were forever bungled by an inept first mate. What is it?
Gilligan's Island is an American sitcom created and produced by Sherwood Schwartz.
Some 40,000 interlocking basalt columns from an ancient volcanic eruption sit on the County Antrim coast of Northern Ireland — a UNESCO World Heritage Site near Bushmills. What's this natural wonder?
Giant's Causeway: Interlocking basalt columns in Northern Ireland
Home of the ancient Vanga Kingdom and the Pala Empire, this South Asian region north of its own namesake bay is today split between Bangladesh and parts of India — what is it?
Bengal: Region in the eastern Indian subcontinent

The highest peak in Washington and the most topographically prominent in the lower 48, this active stratovolcano sits so close to a major city it's ranked among the most dangerous in the world — which mountain?
Mount Rainier: Stratovolcano in the U.S. state of Washington
Founded in San Diego in 1985 and bankrolled at first by its Omnitracs satellite system, this company holds essential patents for 5G and 4G mobile standards — which firm is it?
Qualcomm is an American multinational technology corporation headquartered in San Diego, California.
Born from a bank alliance and once called Interbank and then Master Charge, this Purchase, New York payment-card giant has been publicly traded since 2006 — which company?
Mastercard: American multinational financial services corporation

The second single from Michael Jackson's Thriller tells of a woman insisting the narrator fathered her newborn son — a denial Jackson said echoed groupie claims about his Jackson 5-era brothers. Which song?
Billie Jean: 1983 single by Michael Jackson

Kurt Cobain called it his attempt to write "the ultimate" pop anthem; instead this Nirvana single, opening 1991's Nevermind, is widely marked as the moment grunge crashed into the mainstream. What's the song?
Smells Like Teen Spirit: 1991 single by Nirvana
Arrested 36 times and branded "the most dangerous man in America" by Nixon, this Harvard psychologist founded a Psilocybin Project and became the face of psychedelic advocacy — who was he?

Puccini turned Victorien Sardou's wordy French play into this three-act melodrama set in Napoleon-threatened Rome in 1800 — full of torture, murder, and suicide alongside some of his best-loved arias. Which opera?

First published in 1837 alongside Hans Christian Andersen's "The Little Mermaid," this tale of a vain ruler exposed before his subjects gave us a famous idiom about pretending not to see the obvious. What is it?
The Emperor's New Clothes: 1837 fairy tale by Hans Christian Andersen
H. G. Wells's 1895 novella sends a Victorian scientist hurtling to the year 802,701 — and along the way coined the very term we now use for any such vehicle. What is the book's title?
The Time Machine: 1895 dystopian science fiction novella by H. G. Wells
This Torres Strait Islander's landmark High Court case overturned the doctrine of 'terra nullius' and led to the recognition of native title in Australia — who was he?
Eddie Mabo: Land rights activist for Indigenous Australians (1936–1992)
Fill in the blank: “____ was a kingdom within the Maratha Empire ruled by the Maratha Holkar dynasty.”
Indore State was a kingdom within the Maratha Empire ruled by the Maratha Holkar dynasty.

Nicknamed "Boney," this British general helped plan the tank attack at Cambrai and dreamed up a fully mechanised "Plan 1919" — making this fascist, occultist theorist one of the progenitors of blitzkrieg. Who was he?
J. F. C. Fuller: British Army general (1878–1966)

Also called the Great Abbasid Civil War, this conflict pitted the brothers al-Amin and al-Ma'mun against each other over their father Harun al-Rashid's throne after his death in 809 — which war was it?
Fourth Fitna: Abbasid-era Muslim civil war (811–819)

Stepping into politics after the death of her husband, three-time president Arnulfo Arias, she became this Central American nation's first — and so far only — female president, serving from 1999 to 2004. Who is she?
Mireya Moscoso: President of Panama from 1999 to 2004

A lawyer with no military background, he ruled Guatemala as a dictator for 22 years through controlled elections, modernizing the country while handing sweeping concessions to the American-owned United Fruit Company — who was he?
Manuel Estrada Cabrera: President of Guatemala from 1898 to 1920

Hailed as the "father of the nation," this Papua New Guinean leader was the country's first prime minister after independence and its longest-serving, holding office 17 years across three terms — who was he?
Michael Somare: Papua New Guinean politician (1936–2021)

Born in Atar in French West Africa and a veteran of the Western Sahara War against the Polisario Front, this military officer seized power in a bloodless coup and ruled Mauritania as president from 1984 to 2005 — who is he?
Maaouya Ould Sid'Ahmed Taya: President of Mauritania from 1984 to 2005
A New Brunswick lawyer who became one of the wealthiest Canadians of his era, he later took office as the country's 11th prime minister in 1930 — right as the Depression bit. Who was he?
R. B. Bennett: Prime Minister of Canada from 1930 to 1935

Before politics, this future leader of the Australian Labor Party worked the railways as a qualified engine driver — and went on to serve as Australia's 16th prime minister, defining its post-war reconstruction. Who was he?
Ben Chifley: Prime Minister of Australia from 1945 to 1949

A wealthy Ohio businessman who'd gone to high school alongside John D. Rockefeller, he used his fortune and savvy to mastermind William McKinley's winning presidential campaigns of 1896 and 1900 — who was he?
Mark Hanna: American businessman and politician (1837–1904)
While his crewmates walked the lunar surface, this Apollo 15 command module pilot circled the Moon 74 times alone aboard the Endeavour — who was he?
Alfred Worden: American astronaut and lunar explorer (1932–2020)
With a leg-span of about 3.75 metres, this marine creature boasts the largest reach of any arthropod and is the sole living member of its genus — what is it?
The Japanese giant spider crab (Macrocheira kaempferi) is a species of marine crab and is the largest crab found in the waters around Japan.
This Dutch experimental physicist shared the 1902 Nobel Prize with Hendrik Lorentz for discovering and explaining an effect that now bears his name — who was he?

This American economist gave his name to a model for censored dependent variables — the 'tobit' — and advised the Council of Economic Advisers while championing government action to head off recessions. Who was he?

James Tobin (March 5, 1918 - March 11, 2002) was an American economist who served on the Council of Economic Advisers and consulted with the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, and taught at Yale University.

Studying under Rutherford at the Cavendish Lab, this Adelaide-born physicist discovered the nuclei of helium-3 and tritium and helped achieve the first experimental nuclear fusion — who was this Australian humanitarian?
Beyond the resistance-measuring "bridge" that carries his name, this English inventor also gave us the stereoscope, the English concertina, and the Playfair cipher — who was he?
Charles Wheatstone: English physicist and inventor (1802–1875)

He won a share of the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physics for an effect he discovered as a Cambridge PhD student in 1962 — then, in the 1970s, took up Transcendental Meditation and pursued ideas beyond mainstream science. Who is he?
This South African biologist established the tiny roundworm C. elegans as a model organism, work that helped earn him a share of the 2002 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Who was he?
Sydney Brenner (13 January 1927 - 5 April 2019) was a South African biologist.
This German experimental physicist shared the 1954 Nobel Prize in Physics with Max Born for the 'coincidence method' — the circuitry he used to study the Compton effect and cosmic rays. Who was he?

By measuring weak natural radioactivity with sensitive Geiger counters, this American chemist developed a dating method in 1949 that revolutionized archaeology — and won him a 1960 Nobel Prize. Who was he?
As DuPont's leader of organic chemistry, this American chemist laid the groundwork for neoprene and is credited with inventing one world-changing synthetic fiber — who was he?
Wallace Carothers: American chemist and inventor (1896–1937)

This German fluid dynamicist built the mathematical foundations of subsonic aerodynamics, identifying the 'boundary layer' and lifting-line theory — and lent his name to a dimensionless number. Who was he?
A Scottish biologist-turned-town-planner, he coined the word 'conurbation' and gave us one of the earliest versions of 'think globally, act locally' in social science — who was he?
Patrick Geddes: Scottish scientist and town planner (1854–1932)
Half of the legendary directing duo "the Archers" alongside Michael Powell, this Hungarian-British writer-producer gave us The Red Shoes and A Matter of Life and Death — who was he?
Emeric Pressburger: Hungarian-British screenwriter, director and producer (1902–1988)

Save for Lois Weber, she was the only woman directing in Hollywood from 1927 to 1943, making twenty films and launching the careers of Katharine Hepburn, Rosalind Russell, and Lucille Ball — who was this pioneering filmmaker?
Dorothy Arzner: American film director and film editor (1897–1979)
Once Harun al-Rashid's Abbasid capital around 800 AD, this Syrian city on the Euphrates later served as the Islamic State's capital from 2014 to 2017 — what is it?

Carved from 140-million-year-old granite, this 495-metre Hong Kong peak gets its name from its crouching shape — most striking when viewed from the Choi Hung and San Po Kong areas of East Kowloon. What is it?
Sometimes called the easternmost point of the Polynesian Triangle, this tiny uninhabited Chilean island has stayed nearly untouched by humans thanks to its size and remoteness. Which island is it?
Isla Salas y Gómez, also known as Isla Sala y Gómez, is a small uninhabited Chilean island in the Pacific Ocean.
This Indonesian badminton legend won the All-England men's singles title eight times, including seven years running from 1968 to 1974 — who is he?

The first American woman athlete to become a global celebrity, she won 19 Grand Slam singles titles and helped launch a new tennis fashion of knee-length pleated skirts — which graceful champion was she?

Almost everything we know about this Notre-Dame-school composer comes from an English student called "Anonymous IV" — who credits him with extending Léonin's polyphony into three- and four-part harmony. Which medieval composer is it?

A towering Franco-Flemish composer who served three French kings, his death was mourned in verse by Erasmus and Josquin alike — who was this early-Renaissance master, a bridge between Du Fay and Josquin?

Rising out of 1980s East Village Manhattan, this American conceptual and pop artist made his name by rephotographing and appropriating ads for watches, pens, and living-room furniture to hold a mirror to American culture — who is he?
Richard Prince: American painter and photographer (born 1949)
This Jamaican writer won the 2015 Man Booker Prize for 'A Brief History of Seven Killings' and now teaches literature at Macalester College in Minnesota. Who is he?
Marlon James (born 24 November 1970) is a Jamaican writer.

A self-styled "man of letters" who wrote across everything from urban planning to psychology, this American public intellectual is best remembered for his 1960s works of social criticism urging citizens to act with autonomy and creativity — who was he?
Paul Goodman: American writer and public intellectual (1911–1972)

One of the earliest champions of French Neoclassical architecture, his royally funded buildings came to symbolize the ancien régime — and his visionary "Ideal City of Chaux" earned him a reputation as a utopian. Which architect was he?
Claude Nicolas Ledoux: French Neoclassical architect
After being barred as a woman from London's 1840 World Anti-Slavery Convention, this Quaker preacher helped organize the Seneca Falls Convention and the Declaration of Sentiments. Who was she?
Lucretia Mott (born Coffin; January 3, 1793 - November 11, 1880) was an American Quaker, abolitionist, women's rights activist, and social reformer.

The son of a farm labourer, this English poet sang of the countryside and grieved its disruption, and his biographer Jonathan Bate later crowned him "the greatest labouring-class poet that England has ever produced" — who was he?

The very first writer in England's North American colonies to see her work published, this Puritan poet sailed over with the founders of Massachusetts Bay in 1630 and raised eight children — who was she?
Roy Lichtenstein adapted a 1962 war-comic panel into this 1963 diptych, where a fighter plane's rocket streaks across two canvases to blow up its target — which pop-art masterpiece is it?
Working at the great monastery of Anuradhapura in 5th-century Sri Lanka, this Indian Theravada commentator wrote the Visuddhimagga, or "Path of Purification" — who was he?
Buddhaghosa: Indian Theravadin Buddhist commentator, translator, and philosopher (c. 370–c. 450)

Noël Coward wrote his hit song "Someday I'll Find You" for this 1930 comedy of manners about a divorced couple who, while honeymooning with new spouses, end up in adjacent hotel rooms — what's the play?
Private Lives: 1930 play by Noël Coward
One of New England's "fireside poets" whose work families read aloud at the hearth, this Harvard-trained American was a Romantic poet, critic, editor, and diplomat all in one — who was he?
James Russell Lowell: American poet and diplomat (1819–1891)
Born in Boston, this colonial portrait painter of wealthy New Englanders moved to London in 1774 — never returning to America — and pioneered history paintings in modern dress. Who was he?
John Singleton Copley: American-born British painter (1738–1815)

According to the historian Bede, this Northumbrian cowherd couldn't sing a note until he learned to compose poetry in a dream one night — and went on to become the earliest English poet whose name we know. Who was he?
Dubbed "the bard of American theater," this five-time Tony winner took home Best Play for both "Master Class" and "Love! Valour! Compassion!" Who was he?
In 1912 D. W. Griffith put her on the payroll, making her Hollywood's first female staff screenwriter — but she's best remembered for her 1925 comic novel "Gentlemen Prefer Blondes." Who was she?
Anita Loos: American screenwriter, playwright, author, actress, and television producer
After his "Treatise" "fell dead-born from the press," David Hume reworked his ideas into this shorter, punchier 1748 book to win the public over. What work is it?
An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding: 1748 book by David Hume
A Saxon canoness at Gandersheim Abbey, she's credited as the first female writer of the German-speaking world and the first person since Rome's fall to write drama in the Latin West. Who was she?
This English novelist's third book, "Waterland," swept up the 1983 Guardian Fiction Prize and a Booker shortlist nod. Who is he?
Winner of the National Book Critics Circle Award, this 2001 book was the final novel by German writer W. G. Sebald — what is it?
Austerlitz (novel) — Austerlitz is a 2001 novel by the German writer W.

A Scottish nobleman and poet who first joined the Covenanters but then fought for Charles I, "the Great" one met a grim end — hanged, beheaded, and quartered after his capture at Carbisdale. Who was he?
James Graham, 1st Marquess of Montrose (1612 - 21 May 1650) was a Scottish nobleman, poet, soldier and later viceroy and captain general of Scotland.
A lifelong pacifist from Montana, she was the first woman ever to hold U.S. federal office — and famously the sole member of Congress to vote against war in 1941 — who is it?
Jeannette Rankin: First woman elected to U.S. Congress (1880–1973)

Credited as a 'Father of Cinematography,' this French artist filmed the Roundhay Garden Scene in Leeds in 1888 — then vanished without a trace two years later, and his work never shaped commercial cinema. Who was he?
Louis Le Prince: French motion-picture pioneer (1841–1890s)
The second asteroid ever discovered and likely a leftover protoplanet, this object is the third-largest in the asteroid belt by mass — about 79% the mass of Vesta — what is it?
One of the largest rivers of the eastern Adriatic basin, prized in Bosnia and Croatia for its clear waters and dammed by four hydroelectric plants — which river is it?
Neretva is one of the largest rivers of the eastern part of the Adriatic basin.

A philosophy-loving salonnière of the French Revolution, she ran a husband-and-wife political team to enter public life at a time when women were shut out — and went to the guillotine in 1793. Who was she?
A teacher, barrister and poet, this leader of the 1916 Easter Rising became, after his execution alongside fifteen others, the very embodiment of the rebellion in Irish eyes — who was he?
Written in 121 AD by Hadrian's personal secretary Suetonius, this work collects biographies of Julius Caesar and the first eleven Roman emperors, from Augustus to Domitian — what is it?
On the Lives of the Caesars
The Twelve Caesars: Biographies of Julius Caesar and the first 11 Roman emperors by Suetonius
Fill in the blank: “____ (pinyin: Shjng; Wade-) or the Classic of History, is one of the Five Classics of ancient Chinese literature.”
Book of Documents (pinyin: Shjng; Wade-) or the Classic of History, is one of the Five Classics of ancient Chinese literature.

This variety of Marxism–Leninism, adapted for pre-industrial agricultural China, holds that a united front of progressive forces — not communist revolutionaries alone — leads the revolutionary vanguard. What is it called?
Maoism: Variety of Marxism–Leninism in China
Created by the 1957 Treaty of Rome and renamed when it folded into the EU's first pillar in 1993, which body was popularly known in English as the 'Common Market'?
European Economic Community: Regional organisation from 1958 to 1993
On 30 April 1975, North Vietnamese forces under General Van Tien Dung captured South Vietnam's capital, triggering a frantic evacuation and ending the Vietnam War — what is this event called?
Fall of Saigon was captured by North Vietnam on 30 April 1975.
A French knight who fought alongside Joan of Arc in 1429, this nobleman is chiefly remembered for his later conviction for the rape and murder of numerous children — who was he?
Gilles de Rais: Medieval French nobleman and convicted serial killer

On 26 September 1983, this Soviet duty officer judged his early-warning system's report of incoming U.S. missiles to be a false alarm — disobeying protocol and likely averting nuclear war. Who was he?
The man who saved the world
Stanislav Petrov: Soviet Air Defence Forces officer (1939–2017)

When light from distant objects focuses in front of the retina rather than on it, far-away things blur while close ones stay sharp — and spending more time outdoors as a child seems to lower the risk. What's this refractive error?
Myopia: Inability to focus on distant objects
A Zainichi Korean entrepreneur, this founder and CEO of SoftBank turned a $20 million bet on Alibaba in 2000 into a stake worth around $75 billion — who is he?

Belonging to the ancient order Ephemeroptera and keeping primitive traits like long tails and wings that won't fold flat, which aquatic insect's water-dwelling nymphs signal a clean, unpolluted stream?
Mayfly: Aquatic insects of the order Ephemeroptera
Present in 26 African countries with one of its largest undisturbed populations at Kenya's Lake Turkana, which large crocodilian sees adult males reach 3.5 to 5 metres long?
Spread by rats, dogs and other animals, this bacterial blood infection has an acute, jaundice-causing severe form known as Weil's disease — what's the condition?
Leptospirosis: Blood infection caused by bacteria
A hybrid cross of watermint and spearmint, this herb is one of the oldest used in cooking and medicine and a key plant source of menthol — what is it?
Peppermint: Hybrid flowering plant in the family Lamiaceae
A colorless gas with the formula NO, this free radical carries an unpaired electron and can be brewed by lightning in a thunderstorm. What molecule is it?
Nitric oxide: Colorless gas with the formula NO
Usually caused by a vitamin-D deficiency, this childhood condition softens bones and can produce bowed legs and stunted growth — the adult analogue is osteomalacia; what is it?
A member of the human Herpesviridae family, this contagious pathogen comes in two types, with about 67% of people under 50 carrying the first as of 2016. What is it?
Herpes simplex virus (HSV-1 and HSV-2) are two members of the human Herpesviridae family, a set of viruses that produce viral infections in the majority of humans.
Made of two fused benzene rings, this pungent white crystalline compound is the main ingredient in traditional mothballs — what is it?
As head of Harland and Wolff's drafting department, this shipbuilder helped design the Olympic-class liners and went down with the most famous of them on her maiden voyage — who was he?
Thomas Andrews: British businessman and shipbuilder (1873–1912)
The only mammal that's essentially cold-blooded, this burrowing "sand puppy" of the Horn of Africa also lives in an insect-like colony with a single breeding queen — what creature is it?
A rapid rise-and-fall of voltage across a cell membrane, this "spike" depolarizes neighboring spots and is how neurons and muscle cells fire — what is this electrical event called?
Action potential: Neuron communication by electric impulses
From the Greek for "self-devouring," this lysosome-driven process lets a cell tidily break down and recycle its own worn-out parts — what is it?
Autophagy: Process of cells digesting parts of themselves
Arising from connective tissues like bone, cartilage, muscle and fat, this rare cancer is only about 1% of adult diagnoses but 15% of childhood ones — what is it?
tumor of soft tissue and skeleton
Sarcoma: Cancer originating in connective tissue
Born Lawrence Zeiger, this host went from an all-night Mutual radio call-in show to a nightly CNN interview program that ran from 1985 to 2010 — who was he?
Larry King: American TV and radio host (1933–2021)
This English soprano originated the role of Christine Daaé opposite her then-husband's music, and her 1987 cast album became the biggest-selling cast album ever at 40 million copies — who is she?
Known for 'Let's Play' videos of indie horror games like Five Nights at Freddy's, which American YouTuber ranked as Forbes' third-highest-paid creator on the platform in 2022?
A trained marine biologist who once taught at a marine institute turned his love of the ocean into the fourth longest-running American animated series — which underwater-loving creator dreamed it up?
Stephen Hillenburg: American animator and educator (1961–2018)
The wild-haired promoter behind "The Rumble in the Jungle" and the "Thrilla in Manila" steered the careers of Ali, Foreman, Tyson and Holyfield — who is this boxing impresario?
The Guardian once dubbed him "the great British talkshow host," and his chat show ran in two long stretches from 1971 to 2007 — which knighted presenter was it?
Michael Parkinson: English television and radio personality (1935–2023)
Adapted from the British sitcom Man About the House, this ABC farce had three single roommates platonically sharing a Santa Monica apartment beneath their nosy landlords — which top-10 hit was it?
Once called "the hardest-working man in show business," this host holds the Guinness record for the most hours spent on US television — who is he?
Carved out of colonial Virginia and admitted as the fifteenth state in 1792, this commonwealth earned the 'Bluegrass State' nickname from a species of grass — which state is it?
He coached the Oakland Raiders to a Super Bowl title without ever having a losing season, then won 16 Emmys as an NFL commentator from 1979 to 2009 — which football legend?
John Madden: American football coach and announcer (1936–2021)
This Antiguan batsman, often at number three for a dominant West Indies side, averaged a staggering 66.51 in Tests between 1976 and 1983 — who is this batting great?
A former BBC sports broadcaster and ex-goalkeeper turned author of over 20 books, this Englishman is best known today as a conspiracy theorist — who is he?
The only bowler ever to take 800 Test wickets — and the most in international cricket overall — this Sri Lankan spinner's action stirred endless controversy; who is he?
Founded in 1967 by Herb Kelleher and Rollin King and headquartered at Dallas's Love Field, which major U.S. carrier flies an all-Boeing 737 fleet?
Southwest Airlines: Airline of the United States
Built for continuous DJ sets at 120–150 bpm around a repetitive four-on-the-floor beat, this electronic genre prizes vintage Roland TR-808 and TR-909 drum machines — what is it?
Techno: Genre of electronic dance music
Founded in 1958 by Bank of America as the BankAmericard, this San Francisco company never issues cards itself yet its network processed 257.5 billion transactions in 2025 — which payment giant is it?
Visa Inc.: American payment card services corporation
Born from a 1925 merger of the Holt and C. L. Best tractor companies, this Dow component is the world's largest maker of construction equipment — which CAT-branded firm is it?
Founded in 2011, this Russian feminist collective staged unauthorized guerrilla punk gigs in public places opposing Putin and posted them online as music videos — what's the group?
Published in 1779, this hymn was written by former clergyman John Newton drawing on his own life of twists and redemption, and remains among the most-sung songs in the world — which one is it?
Amazing Grace: 1779 Christian hymn by John Newton
Fill in the blank: “____ is the second of the four canonical Gospels and one of the three Synoptic Gospels.”
Gospel of Mark is the second of the four canonical Gospels and one of the three Synoptic Gospels.
First published in 1830 by Joseph Smith, this scripture claims to record God's dealings with ancient inhabitants of the Americas — what is it?
The Book of Mormon: Another Testament of Jesus Christ
Book of Mormon: Sacred text of the Latter Day Saint movement
When DC let Alan Moore reuse old Charlton characters, an editor talked him into inventing originals instead — yielding which acclaimed 1986–87 comic limited series by Moore and Dave Gibbons?
Watchmen: Comics by Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons
One of the last Australian bushrangers, this gang leader famously faced his final police shootout wearing a homemade suit of bulletproof armour — who was he?
Dubbed 'the most controversial psychoanalyst since Freud,' this French thinker drew crowds to his Paris seminars from 1952 to 1980, with papers later gathered in a volume called Écrits. Who was he?
Jacques Lacan (13 April 1901 - 9 September 1981) was a French psychoanalyst and psychiatrist.
An architect by training who once served as mayor of Quito, this man won Ecuador's presidency on his third try in 1992 after founding a new conservative party — who is it?
Sixto Durán Ballén: President of Ecuador from 1992 to 1996
A multilingual Jewish traveler whose vivid accounts of western Asia preceded Marco Polo's by a full century, he's a major figure in medieval geography — who is it?
Benjamin of Tudela: Jewish explorer and writer (1130–1173)
Brought to Australia as an infant, this geologist joined Shackleton's Nimrod Expedition and became a leading figure of the Heroic Age of Antarctic exploration — who is it?
Douglas Mawson: Australian geologist and explorer of the Antarctic (1882–1958)

A protégé of Robert Walpole, this Whig statesman served as a Secretary of State for 30 unbroken years and dominated British foreign policy — and was twice Prime Minister. By which dukedom is he commonly known?
Thomas Pelham-Holles, 1st Duke of Newcastle: Prime Minister of Great Britain (1754–1756; 1757–1762)
A barrister and journalist elected to Victoria's parliament at just 23, this 'father of Federation' went on to serve three separate terms as Australia's second prime minister — who is it?
Alfred Deakin: Prime Minister of Australia (1903–1904; 1905–1908; 1909–1910)
After lecturing in Nigeria and teaching back home, this man rose to become the longest-serving president in Maldivian history, holding office for 30 years — who is it?
Maumoon Abdul Gayoom: President of the Maldives from 1978 to 2008
This Ohio Republican served in both houses of Congress, was Secretary of the Treasury and of State, and holds the record as Ohio's longest-serving senator at nearly 32 years — who is he?
Elected mayor of Guatemala City six times, this president's crowning achievement was the 1996 peace accord that ended his country's 36-year civil war — who was he?
A slave owner and leading champion of 'popular sovereignty,' he served in the cabinets of Andrew Jackson and James Buchanan and was the 1848 Democratic presidential nominee — who is he?
Lewis Cass: United States Army officer and politician (1782–1866)
This Guinean general seized power in a 1984 coup and then ruled the West African nation as its second president until his death in 2008 — who was he?
Lansana Conté: President of Guinea from 1984 to 2008
Dubbed the 'Father of the Nation,' this Caribbean historian who wrote 'Capitalism and Slavery' led his twin-island country to independence and became its first prime minister — who was he?
Eric Williams: Leader of Trinidad and Tobago from 1956 to 1981
Before circling the Moon 45 times as command module pilot on Apollo 12, this naval aviator had already flown in space piloting Gemini 11 — which astronaut?
Richard F. Gordon Jr.: American astronaut and lunar explorer (1929–2017)
A succulent from the Arabian Peninsula, this popular potted plant stores a soothing gel of acemannan in its leaves — alongside a toxic compound called aloin. What is it?

An annual legume with leaves of three small leaflets, this semiarid crop has flavored dishes of the Indian subcontinent since ancient times — yet there's little clinical proof it works as the supplement people often take. What is it?
This big cat of the genus Panthera prowls the alpine zones of Central and South Asia at elevations of 3,000 to 4,500 meters, from the Himalayas to southern Siberia — what is it?
Snow leopard: Species of large felid
Considered the most renowned Greek mathematician since antiquity, he advanced measure theory and the calculus of variations and even gave thermodynamics an axiomatic formulation — who is it?
This American climatologist's 1988 Congressional testimony helped awaken the public to global warming, and he later turned activist — getting arrested more than once for the cause. Who is it?
This hypothetical element 126, nicknamed eka-plutonium, intrigues physicists because 126 may be a 'magic number' of protons sitting near the center of a predicted island of stability — what is it?
Unbihexium: Theoretical chemical element with atomic number 126 (Ubh)
His 'Essai Sur La Nature Du Commerce' was called the 'cradle of political economy'; this Irish-French banker made a fortune speculating in John Law's Mississippi Company — who is it?
Richard Cantillon: Irish-French economist and banker (c. 1680 – 1734)
This German-born British economist championed 'human-scale, appropriate technology' in his 1973 book, later ranked among the 100 most influential books since World War II — who was he?
E. F. Schumacher: British statistician and economist (1911–1977)

This American climatologist pioneered techniques to pull climate signals from noisy data, building a famous reconstruction of the past thousand years' temperatures with two co-authors in 1998 — who is he?
Michael E. Mann: American physicist and climatologist

About 80% of people who have one of these never feel a thing — but when one blocks the bile duct, it can trigger an intense cramp in the upper-right abdomen known as a "gallbladder attack." What's the culprit?
Gallstone: Disease where stones form in the gallbladder
Holder of 186 patents, this American engineer ran research at General Motors for nearly three decades and gave the world the electric car starter, leaded gasoline, and Freon — who was he?
Charles F. Kettering: American inventor, engineer and businessman (1876–1958)
This 17th-century Dane was a pioneer of both anatomy and geology — he doubted that fossils "grew" in the ground — before becoming a Catholic bishop and being beatified by the Church. Who was he?
Nicolas Steno: Danish scientist and Catholic bishop (1638 – 1686)

This French mathematician reinvented what it means to find the area under a curve, publishing his sweeping new theory of integration in a 1902 dissertation titled "Integral, length, area." Who was he?
Widely credited as the first published Aboriginal Australian author, this Ngarrindjeri preacher also registered 10 patents and toured the country sharing Aboriginal culture — who was he?
Brother of a concert pianist and son of an astronomer, this Russian mathematician built the foundational theory of stability in dynamical systems — who was he?
This American actor won the second-ever Best Actor Oscar for playing the Cisco Kid in 1928's In Old Arizona, and went on to appear in 110 films, starting in the silent era. Who was he?
A former journalist and film critic, this Indonesian director ranges from noir thrillers to the supernatural-horror hit Satan's Slaves and its sequel — who is he?
Joko Anwar: Indonesian filmmaker and actor (born 1976)
In 2006 she played a 'homeschooled teenager' named Bree in YouTube video blogs — until the LA Times revealed the whole thing was fiction, winning her a Webby. Which actress?
In the mid-1930s he was widely seen as the heir to Eugene O'Neill, and his socially charged Depression-era dramas inspired Arthur Miller, Neil Simon, and David Mamet — which playwright?
Clifford Odets: American writer and actor (1906–1963)

In 1980 she co-founded what would become the world's largest animal rights organization, and a year later her partner's monkey photos triggered the first U.S. police raid on a research lab — who is she?
Ingrid Newkirk: British and American animal rights activist (born 1949)
A former journalist and TV publicist, in the 1960s she co-founded the workshop behind a beloved children's show on a New York street — which television producer?
Joan Ganz Cooney: American television writer and producer (born 1929)
Named for its 19th-century founder Sayerr Jobe, this largest metropolitan area in The Gambia grew as businesses fled the cramped island capital of Banjul — what city is it?
Colombia's most active volcano, this 4,276-metre stratovolcano near Pasto turned deadly in 1993, killing six scientists who had climbed into its crater to sample gases — what is it?
Once part of the Nizam's domain and later Hyderabad State, this city in Maharashtra's Marathwada region is home to a Marathwada agricultural university — which city is it?
In 1938 this American became the first tennis player of either sex to sweep all four Grand Slam tournaments in a single year — and was famed for one of the finest backhands the game has seen. Who?
Nicknamed 'Little Mo,' in 1953 she became the first woman to win all four majors in one calendar year, before a horseback riding accident ended her career at 19 — which tennis player?
Famed for her stormy temperament and dramatic intensity, this Spanish singer who sang both contralto and soprano became a legend after dying in Manchester at just 28 — who was she?
The most popular English entertainer of the Regency era, he so defined the harlequinade Clown that the role became known as 'Joey' and his whiteface design is still used by clowns today — who was he?
Joseph Grimaldi: English actor, comedian and dancer
Considered the world's finest classical guitar virtuoso of his day, this Spanish composer wrote an opera at 19 plus didactic studies for guitarists of every level — who was he?
Fernando Sor: Spanish classical guitarist and composer (1778–1839)
In this 1993 Cyan adventure, you click through pre-rendered worlds called "Ages," solving puzzles after a magic book whisks you to a mysterious island — which graphically lush game?

A pupil and friend of Samuel Johnson, this English actor turned heads in the title role of Richard III before buying a share of Drury Lane and reshaping nearly all of 18th-century European theatre — who is it?
David Garrick: English actor, playwright, theatre manager and producer

This British writer moved to South Africa partly because it let her write openly gay characters without the censorship she feared in England — but she's best known for historical novels set in ancient Greece. Under what pen name?
Often called the greatest writer in the Slovene language and sometimes compared to Kafka and Joyce, which playwright-poet helped kick off modernism in Slovene literature?
Ivan Cankar: Slovene writer and political activist (1876–1918)
This American feminist and journalist grew up in rural Nevada and is best known for her sympathetic, on-the-ground coverage of the Bolsheviks during the 1917 Russian Revolution — who is it?
Louise Bryant: American activist and journalist (1885–1936)

Jonathan Lethem: American novelist, essayist, short story writer
Son of Scotland's foremost architect, this neoclassical designer studied for years in Rome and came home to coin a whole namesake 'Style' of architecture and furniture — who is it?

This English poet and novelist is best remembered for his 1947 novel 'Under the Volcano,' voted No. 11 on the Modern Library's 100 Best Novels list — who is he?
Malcolm Lowry: English poet and novelist
Hailed as 'the lady of Brazilian literature,' this São Paulo-born lawyer-turned-novelist explored death, love, fear, and madness, and lived to nearly 104 — who is she?
Lygia Fagundes Telles: Brazilian novelist and writer (1918–2022)

This Scottish educator founded Summerhill in 1924, a school built on freedom from adult coercion and community self-governance, after writing his first book as a diary of his teaching life. Who was he?
A. S. Neill (17 October 1883 - 23 September 1973) was a Scottish educator and author known for his school, Summerhill, and its philosophy of freedom from adult coercion and community self-governance.
This Canadian-born British writer and painter co-founded the Vorticist movement and edited its explosively-named magazine 'Blast,' as well as writing the novel 'Tarr' — who is he?
Wyndham Lewis: English painter and writer (1882–1957)
Honored as 'the author,' this Sephardic rabbi produced the last great codification of Jewish law — the Beit Yosef and its popular distillation, the Shulhan Arukh. Who was he?
Joseph Karo: Spanish rabbi and author on Jewish law (1488–1575)

A master of limewood and stone in Würzburg, this German sculptor of the Late Gothic carved spectacular religious altarpieces, was forgotten after his death, then rediscovered in the 1800s — who is he?
Tilman Riemenschneider: German sculptor and woodcarver (c.1460–1531)

William Lyon Mackenzie: Canadian-American journalist and politician (1795–1861)
Bishop of Lisieux and counselor to King Charles V, this 14th-century French thinker wrote influential works spanning economics, mathematics, physics, astronomy, and theology — who was he?
He called his style 'dynamic cubism' and found his subjects in everyday Harlem life, portraying African-American history with blacks and browns beside vivid color — which painter?
A 1963 pop-art 'masterpiece of melodrama' showing a teary woman on a turbulent sea, based on comic-book art and ranked alongside Lichtenstein's 'Whaam!' — which painting?

Fill in the blank: “____ (Aquila audax) is the largest bird of prey in the continent of Australia.”
Wedge-tailed eagle (Aquila audax) is the largest bird of prey in the continent of Australia.

Gerhard Schröder: Chancellor of Germany from 1998 to 2005
On a single day in August 1071, the Seljuks crushed a Byzantine army and even captured Emperor Romanos IV — a defeat that opened the door to the gradual Turkification of Anatolia. Which clash was it?

Cambodian–Vietnamese War: 1978–89 conflict between Vietnam and the Khmer Rouge
From a Sanskrit word literally meaning 'descent,' this Hindu concept signifies a powerful deity's incarnation on Earth, often in human form — what is it called?
Avatar: Incarnation of a god on Earth in Hinduism
Formed by a 1928 merger of a French electrical-engineering firm and a Thomson-Houston subsidiary, which company today builds high-speed trains, trams, and rail signalling?

Nestor Ivanovych Makhno, also known as Bat'ko Makhno, was a Ukrainian anarchist revolutionary and the commander of the Revolutionary Insurgent Army of Ukraine during the Ukrainian War of Independence.
The simplest stable amino acid, with just a single hydrogen for a side chain, it's the only common one that isn't chiral and makes up about 35% of collagen — what is it?
Glycine (symbol Gly or G) is an organic compound with the formula C2H5NO2, and is the simplest stable amino acid, distinguished by having a single hydrogen atom as its side chain.
A person with this condition becomes unduly alarmed by even the most minor symptom, convinced a serious illness is upon them despite no medical diagnosis — what is it?
Hypochondriasis: Excessive fear of developing illness

Metastasis is the spread of a pathogenic agent from an initial or primary site to a different or secondary site within the host's body; the term is typically used when referring to metastasis by a cancerous tumor.
Fill in the blank: “____ (Chrysocyon brachyurus) is a large canine of South America.”
Maned wolf (Chrysocyon brachyurus) is a large canine of South America.
Long before chemists called it 3,4,5-trimethoxyphenethylamine, this psychedelic was drawn from peyote and San Pedro cacti for spiritual ceremonies — which naturally occurring compound is it?

Arginine is the amino acid with the formula (H2N)(HN)CN(H)(CH2)3CH(NH2)CO2H.
This Hungarian-American biochemist spent years fighting skepticism over messenger RNA before her groundwork made mRNA vaccines possible, earning a shared 2023 Nobel Prize — who is she?
Refined from bauxite and nicknamed alumina, this compound shows up in nature as the mineral corundum — the very stuff of rubies and sapphires. What is it?

John Money: New Zealand psychologist and sexologist (1921–2006)

Ammonoidea: Extinct subclass of cephalopod molluscs
Born William Frederick Cody, this Old West soldier and bison hunter founded a traveling 'Wild West' show in 1883 that toured America and, from 1887, Europe — who is it?
Buffalo Bill: American soldier and showman (1846–1917)

John Oliver: British and American comedian (born 1977)

This landlocked South Central state takes its name from the Choctaw words for 'people' and 'red,' and borders Texas, Kansas, and Arkansas — which state is it?
Perched on a desert plateau over 400 metres above the western shore of the Dead Sea, this fortress complex was transformed into a fortified refuge by Herod the Great — what is it?
Masada: Ancient hilltop fortification in Israel
Built on Toronto's former Railway Lands and named for the railway that raised it, this 553-metre spire reigned as the world's tallest free-standing structure for 32 years. What is it?
The CN Tower is a 553.3-metre-high (1,815.3 ft) communications and observation tower in Toronto, Ontario, Canada.
Bordered by the Mississippi to the east and the Missouri and Big Sioux to the west, this landlocked Midwestern state has Des Moines as its capital. Which state is it?
Iowa is a landlocked state in the upper Midwestern region of the United States.

Orkney: Archipelago, county and council area in northern Scotland

The Motherland Calls: Volgograd monumental sculpture

Lawrence Peter "Yogi" Berra was an American professional baseball catcher who later took on the roles of manager and coach.
A left-handed Dodger for all 18 of his seasons, this three-time Cy Young winner became one of just four southpaws ever in the 3,000-strikeout club. Who is he?
Clayton Kershaw (born March 19, 1988) is an American former professional baseball pitcher who played 18 seasons for the Los Angeles Dodgers of Major League Baseball (MLB).

This Japanese electronics giant takes its name from a 1939 merger and its former identity, Tokyo Shibaura Denki — which company keeps quantum cryptography on the same product list as elevators and hard drives?

Gospel of Luke is the third of the New Testament's canonical Gospels.

Magical realism: Style of literary fiction and art

Eckhart Tolle (TOL-;; born Ulrich Leonard Tlle, 16 February 1948) is a German "spiritual teacher" and self-help author.
This Odawa war chief led Native Americans against the British in the Great Lakes region from 1763 to 1766, in a conflict that came to bear his name — who was he?

Piye: Ancient Kushite king and pharaoh

Edward Coke (CUUK, formerly; 1 February 1552 - 3 September 1634) was an English barrister, judge, and politician.

Isabelle Eberhardt: Swiss explorer and writer
Starting in his father's grocery business, this English industrialist built an empire on Sunlight Soap and brands like Lux and Lifebuoy through the firm he founded with his brother — who was he?
William Lever, 1st Viscount Leverhulme: English industrialist, philanthropist and politician (1851–1925)

Born free in Virginia, this merchant emigrated to a young West African colony in 1829 and went on to become the first man of African descent to govern Liberia as its first president — who is it?

Jules Dumont d'Urville: French explorer and naval officer (1790–1842)

Chickpea: Species of flowering plant with edible seeds

A short evergreen shrub with dull green leaves and orange-red berries, this nightshade-family plant is better known by names like Indian ginseng and winter cherry — what is it?
Withania somnifera: Species of flowering plant

The first woman to officially attend a Dutch university, she became one of the Netherlands' earliest female physicians and, in 1882, opened the world's first birth control clinic — who was this suffrage leader?
Aletta Jacobs (Dutch; 9 February 1854 - 10 August 1929) was a Dutch physician and women's suffrage activist.
Dubbed "the father of supercomputing," this American engineer founded a company bearing his name and built machines that were the fastest in the world for decades — who was he?

Lynn Conway: American computer scientist and electrical engineer (1938–2024)
A Ming-dynasty naturalist poured 27 years into a sprawling pharmacology compendium of nearly 1,900 entries, 11,000 prescriptions, and over a thousand herbs — who was this herbalist and physician?
Li Shizhen (July 3, 1518 - 1593), courtesy name Dongbi, was a Chinese acupuncturist, herbalist, naturalist, pharmacologist, physician, and writer of the Ming dynasty.

Laura Bassi: Italian physicist and academic (1711–1778)

Yarlung Tsangpo: River flowing through China and India

Tirunesh Dibaba (born 1 June 1985) is an Ethiopian long-distance runner athlete who competes in long-distance track events and international road races.

Don Hutson: American football player and coach (1913–1997)

Herbert Chapman: English association football player and manager (1878–1934)

Ambient 1: Music for Airports: 1979 studio album by Brian Eno

Katherine Dunham (June 22, 1909 - May 21, 2006) was an American dancer, choreographer, anthropologist, and social activist.
Composer, engineer, and broadcaster, this Frenchman founded a research group devoted to musique concrète and is recognized as a pioneer of experimental electronic music. Who was he?

A colorless salt that looks unnervingly like sugar but tastes acrid and bitter, this compound is mostly used in gold mining and electroplating — and just 200 to 300 milligrams will kill nearly any human. What is it?

In this lung disease the walls between the alveoli break down, merging tiny air sacs into enlarged spaces that shrink the surface available for gas exchange and starve the blood of oxygen. Which condition is it?
The 'Blonde Bomber' won four Super Bowls in six years with the Steelers — the first quarterback ever to claim three and then four rings — and later became a Fox NFL Sunday co-host. Who is he?
Terry Bradshaw (born September 2, 1948) is an American former professional football quarterback who played in the National Football League (NFL) for 14 seasons with the Pittsburgh Steelers.
Crowned the "Queen of Burlesque" for almost single-handedly reviving the art form, which performer is also remembered for a brief marriage to Marilyn Manson?
Dita Von Teese: American vedette, burlesque dancer, model, and businesswoman
Soldier, scout, lawman, gambler and showman, this Old West folk hero saw his fame inflated by tall tales he sometimes printed about himself — who was he?
Wild Bill Hickok: American folk hero and lawman (1837–1876)
Airing on NBC nearly every weekday since November 1965 and now streaming on Peacock, this is one of the longest-running scripted programs in the world — what soap opera is it?
Days of Our Lives: American daytime television soap opera (since 1965)
The Columbia River traces much of its northern edge, the Snake its eastern, and the 42nd parallel its southern line with California and Nevada — while the Pacific forms its west. Which state is it?
Nicknamed 'the General,' this men's college basketball coach won three NCAA titles at Indiana and retired with a then-record 902 Division I wins — who was he?
Its two-minute-twelve-second guitar coda was voted the best solo of all time by Guitarist readers in 1998, and the track won the Grammy for Record of the Year — which 1977 Eagles single is it?
Formed in 1961 Detroit as The Elgins, this Motown group's 1968 hit "Cloud Nine" helped pioneer psychedelic soul — which five-man vocal act, famed for its choreography and harmonies, is it?
The Temptations: American rhythm and blues group
Founded in Sydney in 1991, this Australian children's music group is famous for its color-coded performers and skivvies — who are they?
The Wiggles: Australian children's music group
Born in 1999 from a merger and descended from John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil, this Texas-headquartered giant is the largest investor-owned oil company in the world. Which corporation?
ExxonMobil is an American multinational oil and gas corporation headquartered in Spring, Texas, a suburb of Houston.
Founded in New York in 1849 by two German entrepreneurs, this is one of the oldest pharmaceutical companies in North America, with top sellers like Eliquis and Paxlovid — what company is it?
Pfizer: American multinational pharmaceutical and biotechnology corporation

Born Singanalluru Puttaswamaiah Muthuraj, this towering Kannada cinema actor and singer earned nicknames like "Emperor of Actors" and "Man of Gold" and a Padma Bhushan in 1983. Who was this Indian icon?
Dr. Rajkumar (24 April 1929 - 12 April 2006), better known by his stage name Dr.
A British-naturalised Russian FSB defector and fierce Putin critic, he coined the phrase "mafia state" — which former security officer is this?
This 55.5 cm bronze fountain in central Brussels depicts a nude boy doing exactly what its Dutch name says — and has been stolen so often that the original now sits in a museum. What is it?
Manneken Pis: Brass sculpture and fountain in Brussels, Belgium

A Somali scholar and poet who'd memorized the entire Quran, he founded the Dervish movement against British, Italian, and Ethiopian colonizers — and the British insultingly dubbed him the 'Mad Mullah.' Who was he?
Muḥammad ibn 'Abdallāh Hassan: Somali Jihadist and anti-colonialist leader (1856–1920)
He ruled an isolated pocket of Roman authority around Soissons long after the empire lost the region, until the Frankish king Clovis I defeated and killed him — who was this last Roman holdout?
Syagrius: 5th century Roman leader at Soissons
One of only two men to serve as Secretary of State under three presidents, this Maine statesman won the 1884 Republican nomination but narrowly lost the White House — who was he?
Succeeding Sani Abacha upon his death, this Nigerian general steered the country to multiparty elections and handed power to Olusegun Obasanjo in 1999 — who was he?
Abdulsalami Abubakar (born 13 June 1942) is a retired Nigerian army general who served as the military head of state of Nigeria from 1998 to 1999.

Nicknamed the "Penman of the Constitution," this Founding Father wrote its famous Preamble, championed the radical idea of being a citizen of one united nation rather than just a state, and was an outspoken foe of slavery — who was he?
Gouverneur Morris: American Founding Father and politician
A member of the Fang ethnic group who began as a colonial customs agent, he became the first Prime Minister and then President of Gabon, serving until his death in 1967 — who was he?
Léon M'ba: Prime Minister (1959–61) and President (1961–67) of Gabon
Imprisoned and tortured as a young dissident under the Ottomans and once sentenced to death by the French, he went on to become the first president of independent Syria in 1943 — who was he?
Born in modern-day Gabon, he served as Minister of Defense under Bokassa before seizing power and ruling the Central African Republic from 2003 to 2013 — who is he?
François Bozizé: President of the Central African Republic from 2003 to 2013
Born a princess, this Indian independence activist became free India's first Health Minister in 1947, championed women's rights, and founded the National Institute of Sports — who was she?
A rags-to-riches Western Han general celebrated for his campaigns against the Xiongnu, he rose through ties to Emperor Wu and was uncle to the famed general Huo Qubing — who was he?
A striking red-capped, white-warted mushroom of northern forests, this fungus may owe its name to an old use against flies — or to a medieval belief that flies caused madness. What is it?
This German mathematician's 1872 Erlangen program reorganized all of geometry by its underlying symmetry groups, and he later turned Göttingen into a world center of research — who was he?
This British economist won the 1991 Nobel Memorial Prize and warned that the field was "suicidal" to become a hard science of choice while ignoring society, history, and culture — who was he?
Ronald Coase (29 December 1910 - 2 September 2013) was a British economist and author.
This Russian engineer-polymath gave the world its first hyperboloid towers and diagrid shells — and, as a side project, invented an early oil-cracking method — who was he?
Vladimir Shukhov: Russian polymath, engineer, scientist and architect (1853–1939)
He won the Fields Medal in 1954 and, nearly half a century later, the very first Abel Prize in 2003 — which French mathematician of algebraic topology and geometry is it?

For decades this University of Virginia psychiatrist ran a Division of Perceptual Studies and gathered evidence that memories — and even bodily features — might carry across lives. Which researcher into reincarnation was he?

Ian Stevenson (October 31, 1918 - February 8, 2007) was a Canadian-born American psychiatrist, the founder and director of the Division of Perceptual Studies at the University of Virginia School of Medicine.
Element 121, this not-yet-synthesized superactinide is expected to open a brand-new g-block of the periodic table and may sit on the 'island of stability' — what's its placeholder name?
Unbiunium: Theoretical chemical element with atomic number 121 (Ubu)
This French inventor born near Toulouse is remembered chiefly as an aviation pioneer, but in 1870 he was also among the first to take up the sport of cycling in France — who is it?
Clément Ader: French inventor and engineer (1841–1925)
Often called the first screenwriter to succeed as a director, he sold the story for 'The Great McGinty' to Paramount for just $10 in exchange for the chance to direct it — who is it?
Preston Sturges: American film director and screenwriter
The New York Times once called him the country's best-known lawyer; this civil rights attorney is most famous for defending the Chicago Seven — who is it?
William Kunstler: American attorney and civil rights activist (1919–1995)
With her smash Valley of the Dolls and two follow-ups, she became the first author ever to top the New York Times bestseller list with three consecutive novels — who was she?
Jacqueline Susann: American novelist and actress (1918–1974)
This Canadian-born comedian left home at 14, built a Broadway career on improvised laughs, and became a Hollywood favorite in silent and Depression-era films — who was she?
The third-largest island in the Philippines, first sighted by Magellan in 1521, is split into three Waray-speaking provinces and celebrates June 19 as a holiday — what is it?
The state capital of Kedah, Malaysia sits on the main corridor toward Thailand and is home to the country's third-tallest tower — which city is it?
Alor Setar: State capital of Kedah, Malaysia
This volcanic range in the central Sahara, mostly in northern Chad, is crowned by Emi Koussi — the highest point in both Chad and the entire Sahara — what is it?
Tibesti Mountains: Mountain range in the Sahara
Opened in 1925 after the last emperor was evicted, this Beijing complex fills the Forbidden City's 980 buildings with over 1.8 million artworks from the Ming and Qing dynasties — what is it?
The Palace Museum, also known as the Beijing Palace Museum, is a large national museum complex housed in the Forbidden City at the core of Beijing, China.
He didn't invent the blues but, by being among the first to publish it in print, he lifted the genre from a regional Delta style to national fame — which self-styled 'Father of the Blues' is it?
W. C. Handy: American blues composer and musician (1873–1958)

Kraftwerk's sixth album, recorded in 1976 Düsseldorf, traded warmth for sequenced rhythms and minimalism while musing on the gap between reality and appearance — and celebrating the European railway service it's named for. Which album?
Trans-Europe Express is the sixth studio album by German electronic band Kraftwerk.
Often called the greatest Polish composer since Chopin, he wrote four symphonies and a Concerto for Orchestra — but, tellingly, never an opera — who is this 20th-century composer and conductor?
Witold Lutosławski: Polish composer and conductor (1913–1994)

In just five sessions between 1927 and 1930 this street preacher recorded 30 gospel-blues songs whose chest-voice power and slide guitar shaped generations — yet he died with little wealth. Who was he?
Blind Willie Johnson: American gospel blues musician (1897–1945)
Called 'The Voice of the Civil Rights Movement,' this folk and spirituals singer counted Rosa Parks as her number-one fan and influenced Dylan, Baez, and Joplin — who went by a single name?
Best known for 14 comic operas written with the dramatist W. S. Gilbert — including The Mikado — this English composer also penned 'Onward, Christian Soldiers' and 'The Lost Chord.' Who was he?
Taken in and cultured by the literary Sitwell siblings, this Lancashire-born composer wrote Belshazzar's Feast and the coronation marches Crown Imperial and Orb and Sceptre — who was he?

Critic Alex Ross claimed no recent classical composer had as much commercial success as this Polish figure of the post-Stalin avant-garde, whose dissonant 1950s works were shaped by the influence of Anton Webern — who is it?
Crowned the 'Father of the Texas blues,' this 1920s singer's high-pitched voice and original guitar work made him so distinctive that rivals couldn't easily imitate him — who is it?
Blind Lemon Jefferson: American blues musician (1893–1929)

Born into a Boston Brahmin family that traced back to the Mayflower, this poet mythologized New England and named Allen Tate, Elizabeth Bishop, and William Carlos Williams as his unlikely trio of influences — who is he?
Its Greek title translates roughly to 'Lectures on Nature,' and it survives within the Corpus Aristotelicum attributed to a 4th-century BC philosopher — which foundational text is it?

Physics (Aristotle) — Physics (Ancient) is a named text, written in ancient Greek, collated from a collection of surviving manuscripts known as the Corpus Aristotelicum, attributed to the 4th-century BC philosopher Aristotle.

A painter, philosopher and social commentator who befriended Coleridge, Wordsworth and Keats, this English essayist is now ranked alongside Samuel Johnson and George Orwell despite being little read today. Who?
William Hazlitt (10 April 1778 - 18 September 1830) was an English essayist, drama and literary critic, painter, social commentator, and philosopher.

Born in Pennsylvania at the dawn of the oil boom, this pioneering muckraker turned her McClure's series into The History of the Standard Oil Company, called the most influential business book ever published. Who was she?
Ida Tarbell: American writer, journalist, biographer and lecturer (1857–1944)
This second emperor of Vietnam's Trần dynasty handed the throne to his son yet stayed on as 'retired emperor,' co-commanding the victories that repelled two Mongol invasions of Đại Việt — who was he?
Trần Thánh Tông: Emperor of Đại Việt from 1258 to 1278

America's first female war correspondent and full-time book reviewer, this transcendentalist wrote what's considered the first major feminist work in the U.S., Woman in the Nineteenth Century — who was she?
Margaret Fuller: American writer and women's activist (1810–1850)
He spent most of his life as an insurance executive in Hartford while writing modernist poems like 'The Emperor of Ice-Cream' and 'Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird' — which American poet?
This Lake Poet and Poet Laureate, who drifted from radical to conservative, is remembered for 'After Blenheim' and for writing the original version of 'Goldilocks and the Three Bears' — who is he?
Briefly Ghana's Secretary for Education, she became the first published female African dramatist with her 1965 play The Dilemma of a Ghost and later won the Commonwealth Writers' Prize — who is she?
Ama Ata Aidoo: Ghanaian writer, politician, and academic (1942–2023)
Often called the first female career artist in Western Europe — supporting her family of 11 children on commissions, with her husband as agent — which Bologna-born Mannerist painter is it?
Hailed as the father of modern Armenian literature for a novel written in the everyday Yerevan dialect, this polymath educator mysteriously vanished in 1848 — who was he?
Khachatur Abovian: Armenian polymath and writer (1809–1848?)
This Alsatian artist published over 140 books — children's tales, biting satire, political and film posters alike — and won the Hans Christian Andersen Medal in 1998. Who was he?
Tomi Ungerer: French artist and writer (1931–2019)
This American mystery writer spun 33 novels and dozens of novellas around a brilliant detective and his sidekick Archie Goodwin, earning the Grand Master Award — who was he?
This English novelist edited The English Review and The Transatlantic Review, but is best remembered for The Good Soldier and the Parade's End tetralogy — who was he?
Ford Madox Ford: English writer and publisher (1873–1939)
One of the nine canonical Greek lyric poets, this man was reputedly the bitter rival of Pindar and the uncle of Bacchylides, and Lessing later dubbed him "the Greek Voltaire" — who is he?
Simonides of Ceos: Greek lyric poet (c. 556–468 BC)

Fill in the blank: “____ (July 1, 1893 - March 21, 1955) was an American civil rights activist who led the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) for a quarter of a century, from 1929 until 1955.”
Walter Francis White was an American civil rights activist who led the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People for a quarter of a century, from 1929 until 1955.
This poet from Zakynthos wrote the Hymn to Liberty, which became the national anthem of both Greece and Cyprus — earning him the title of Greece's national poet. Who was he?
A key figure in the 'confessional' school, this American poet won the 1965 Pulitzer for his 77 Dream Songs — who was he?
John Berryman: American poet and scholar (1914–1972)
For decades this film critic's annual book of capsule reviews was a movie-lover's bible, and he reviewed films on Entertainment Tonight from 1982 to 2012 — who is he?
Leonard Maltin: American film critic and film historian (born 1950)
Over 57 years with UPI, this reporter covered the White House through ten presidents, from Kennedy to Obama, becoming the first female officer of the National Press Club — who was she?
Helen Thomas (August 4, 1920 - July 20, 2013) was an American reporter and author, and a long-serving member of the White House press corps.
This English novelist practically invented the Regency romance, yet after These Old Shades sold well during the General Strike she swore off publicity and never gave an interview again — who was she?
Born Cecily Fairfield, this British author covered the Nuremberg trials in A Train of Powder and wrote the sweeping Yugoslavia study Black Lamb and Grey Falcon — under what pen name?
Rebecca West: British author and journalist (1892–1983)
Pen name of Zhao Zhenkai and a perennial Nobel candidate, this dissident poet leads the school the West dubbed 'Misty' or 'Obscure' poetry — who is he?
Imprisoned for joining the November Uprising yet writing over 200 novels, this prolific Polish author spent his later years in Dresden championing Polish independence — who was he?
Józef Ignacy Kraszewski (28 July 1812 - 19 March 1887) was a Polish novelist, journalist, historian, publisher, painter, and musician.
A leading anarchist, lifelong friend and onetime lover of Emma Goldman, he made a failed 1892 attempt to assassinate businessman Henry Clay Frick as 'propaganda of the deed' — who was he?
Alexander Berkman: Russian-American anarchist and writer (1870–1936)
Her 1950 collection Annie Allen made her the first African American ever to win the Pulitzer Prize; later she became Poet Laureate of Illinois for over three decades — who was she?

Famous for the ideas of "bounded rationality" and "satisficing," this remarkable scholar won both a Turing Award and a Nobel in Economics — bridging computer science, economics, and psychology. Who was he?
Herbert A. Simon: American academic and Nobel Laureate (1916–2001)
Which Filipino-American journalist, co-founder and CEO of Rappler, won the Nobel Peace Prize after nearly two decades as a lead investigative reporter for CNN in Southeast Asia?
Maria Ressa (Tagalog; ne Delfin Aycardo; born October 2, 1963) is a Filipino and American journalist and Nobel Peace Prize laureate.
Born into an aristocratic Prussian military family, this German field marshal of World War II was later convicted of war crimes and sentenced to 18 years' imprisonment. Who was he?
Fritz Erich Georg Eduard von Manstein
Erich von Manstein: German field marshal (1887–1973)
Formally revealed to non-Nazi leaders at the January 1942 Wannsee Conference near Berlin, this was the official Nazi code name for the murder of all Jews within reach — what was it called?
Final Solution to the Jewish question
Final Solution: Nazi plan for the genocide of Jews

Ruling Panama from 1983 to 1989 through puppet presidents while amassing a fortune in drug trafficking, this dictator was ousted by a U.S. invasion despite past ties to American intelligence — who was he?
Manuel Noriega: Military dictator of Panama from 1983 to 1989
